name: porting-workflow
description: "The principles a port campaign follows and where it differs from binding: Rust consumers, tests tied to modules, one language per module, a module's switch from C to Rust and its builds. Read before porting a module or integrating one."
---

# Porting workflow

How a `port` campaign proceeds. It follows the [binding workflow](../binding-workflow/SKILL.md) throughout;
this document gives the principles a port follows and where it differs. How each item is
ported is [`porting`](../../rust/porting/SKILL.md).

## 1. Principles

### 1.1 Rust consumers

A port produces a Rust library for Rust-native applications. Its public API is the safe
Rust one; the installed C headers and the C ABI they describe are not kept for C
applications outside the target. The crate bundles the C that remains, as
[`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes, so that a consumer has the whole
library and reaches what is not ported yet through its raw bindings.

A ported module's C-facing surface is only what the target's own remaining C still
consumes, its translation units, tests and executables alike: its `extern "C"` exports,
under their bare C names, through which that C calls the Rust that replaced the module. The
remaining C depends on the Rust, never the Rust on a C copy of a ported module, so that
each function has one implementation and each global one copy. The surface shrinks as that
C is ported.

A type, public or internal, therefore keeps its C layout, and its `wrap`, only while
unported C of the target accesses that layout. The target's tests do not count, as
[Tests follow their modules](#12-tests-follow-their-modules) describes, and neither does a
definition in an installed header: the C consumers it would serve are outside the target.

### 1.2 Tests follow their modules

Each module carries the C tests tied to it, those whose subject it is, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Bundling section describes.
They assert the C contract, which a safe Rust implementation may change. Those that reach
the module's internals run while it is C and leave with it at its switch. Those that
use only its public API stay, and check its exports, which keep that contract for the C
that calls them, until their `port/unexport` carries them over, as the
[conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes. The tests its
port batches write mirror their regression cases, as
[`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s C tests carried over section describes. A
test's access to a module's internals is a use within that module, so it never keeps a type
wrapped.

A C test that only calls a module, to set up or tear down its fixtures, is not tied to it:
once the module has switched, the test reaches it through its exports, so that it checks
its own subject with the ported Rust under it, as part of the integration regression gate. A
test never keeps an export the remaining C no longer needs: the export's `port/unexport`
carries over the test cases that still reference it, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section describes.

A test whose subject is several modules is tied to each of them, and leaves at the first
point at which it would leave as a test of one of them alone. Each ported module's own
tests cover it from then on.

A test case whose body the configured build compiles empty, under a configuration the
target is built without, such as `GIT_WIN32`, tests nothing of the target: it is out of
scope, as a configured-out translation unit is, tied to no module and holding nothing back.

### 1.3 One language per module

A module is in one language at a time. The campaign maintains C and Rust side by side, but
on disjoint modules, never the same code in both.

While the waves of a module's `wrap` and `port` items run, its C is the reference its
ports are tested against, and the target is built and linked from C alone.
Once the last of them has landed, the module switches to Rust, once, as [Builds](#3-builds)
describes: the Rust module replaces the TU in the target's link, its C is removed from the
build and from the tree, and its tests switch with it. The removal is made on the working branch; the shipping branch keeps the C until
the user approves shipping the module. From then on the module is Rust's: what it still
keeps for the remaining C, its types' C layouts and storage and its exports, its later
stages remove after the switch, as [Later stages](#4-later-stages) describes.

The headers bundled with the module stay while remaining C includes them, declaring the
module's exports, its `static inline` functions included, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../rust/porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Static inline functions section describes, and go with the last C
file that includes them.

The module's equivalence tests, which need the C, are retired with it, and the behaviour
they established is kept by its unit tests. Before the module's equivalence tests are
retired, each that needs no C is carried over to the module's unit tests, where what it
compares with stays after the switch, such as the constants of a header that remaining C
still includes. The raw bindings of its
exported functions and globals then reach its exports, so that a consumer's raw calls keep
working, and an allowlist entry goes with the export it reaches. Those of its functions and
globals that have no export, which only its own C referenced, are removed with their
allowlist entries at the switch.

A ported module's items therefore reach the rest of its module natively from the start:
an edge within a module needs neither a `wrap` binding nor an export, only the edges that
leave it.

## 2. Batches

A port campaign's schedule mixes both kinds of batch, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s
Waves and batches section describes: a selected symbol is `port` from the start, a
selected type is `wrap` while another module's unported C depends on its layout and `port`
once none does, and a dependency outside the selected migration set stays `wrap`. A type
whose layout only its own module and tests use is `port` from the start. Each batch runs
the agent its objective names, in the same waves.

## 3. Builds

A module's waves do not change the compiled target. Its `port` batches add Rust that is
built and tested on its own, against the target's C build, which still compiles the
module's C and links no Rust: there is no build switch, and no batch flips one. The
module's `ffi_export` gateway is written with its items but compiled only under its export
feature, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports and Export features sections
describe, which stays off, so its bare-named exports never collide with the C the tests
link. Native Rust items carry mangled names and cannot collide with it.

The C stays until the switch: the target's other C still calls the module's symbols, which
only the exports could define, and the module's equivalence tests and its cut cycles still
run through it.

Once the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port` items has landed, it switches
in one step, with concurrent modules as part of its branch's integration into the working
branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Integration section
describes: its export feature is deleted, so that its gateway compiles from then on, its TU
and the C tests tied to it that reach its internals are removed from `c/`, and the
remaining C reaches the module through its exports. The C side of the
step is a commit on the fork's `main`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section
describes, and the campaign's commit records the submodule at it: integrations run one at a
time, so the two repositories move together.

The step's parts run in this order, both sides before the builds:

1. The Rust side, in one commit. The module's export feature is deleted, its equivalence
   tests are retired, those that need no C carried over first, the allowlist entries of its
   functions and globals that have no export are removed, and the bindings are regenerated
   against the builds in use, whose headers the switch does not change.
   Deleting the feature removes or rewrites every mention of its name in the crate, in its
   sources, its tests, its manifest and its build script, a `cfg_attr` or a `cfg(any(…))`
   as much as the gateway's attribute: an unknown `cfg`, or a lint expectation left unmet,
   fails the lints with warnings denied.
2. The C side: the module's TU and its tied C tests leave the fork.
3. The builds, from the C that remains. Each variant is configured, the Rust library is
   built, then the C is built and linked: the C that remains links the module's exports,
   which the Rust library holds only once the export feature is deleted.
4. The gates, over those builds.

From then on, the C that remains is linked in two ways, and no process holds a module both
as C and as Rust, nor its Rust twice:

- a Rust consumer, the campaign's own tests included, links the safe crate and the C that
  remains, which the crate bundles, statically or as shared libraries, as the raw bindings'
  Build modes describe; and
- the target's remaining C consumers, its C tests and executables, link the C that remains
  and the safe crate's Rust static library, built in campaign mode so that it carries no C
  of its own, through the target's actual build system.

The C tests that remain run over that second link as the integration regression gate, as
[`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes.
For that link, the first switch changes the fork's C build so that the remaining C's
tests and executables link the safe crate's Rust library, static or shared, in the build
system's own idiom, and each later switch takes its module's C out of that build.

## 4. Later stages

A module switches once. Its later-stage waves, `port/layout`, `port/memory` and
`port/unexport`, run after its switch, each once the switches its release point
waits for have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section times them: as the remaining C stops using its types' layouts and storage and
calling its exports, they nativize the types and remove the exports. They belong to no run
of the module and integrate nothing: each forks from the working branch and is promoted
back to it, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Lifecycle section
describes. A stage changes no C, since the C that held it back has left the build, but for
what still names the export a `port/unexport` removes. That
change is a commit on the fork's `main`, which the stage's commit records, as a switch's
is, and the stage's C tests run over variants built from the C it leaves, as
[Builds](#3-builds) describes for a switch.

## 5. Scope

The unit of a port is a module: its scope is whole modules, the foundational ones
included, which stay `wrap`, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational modules section
describes. Porting a few named items without their module is not described.

# Testing

Tests are classified by what decides them and by the side of a module they test, and each
is placed where the conventions' Testing section places tests of its kind:

- UB tests on the safe public interface show that it does not reach UB, mainly by not
  triggering sanitizer or Miri crashes, or by failing to compile for a given illegal path;
- UB tests on the unsafe public interface target UB there: each public `unsafe fn` or
  method a workset adds, called within its stated `# Safety` contract, edge cases
  included. Raw `sys::` round-trips are not UB tests on the unsafe interface; they are unit
  or equivalence tests;
- equivalence tests show that the Rust behaves as the C it translates, mainly by passing
  equivalence assertions: `equiv_pub` on the module's exported API, `equiv_priv` on its
  internals; and
- unit tests show that the Rust keeps its contract, by passing Rust assertions, without
  the C: `unit_pub` on the public interface, `unit_priv` on the internal routines.

<!-- TODO: fuzzing, of the safe public interface and differentially against the C, is
deferred. -->

Test objects are constructed through safe constructors. The UB tests on the safe public
interface use the safe API alone, their suite forbidding `unsafe_code` at its root: a type
that no safe constructor or producer yields yet gets those tests in the batch that wraps
its first one. Elsewhere, while a type has no safe constructor, one documented unsafe
fixture per type adopts the raw constructor's result, and is replaced once the safe
constructor exists.

A test exercises the safe API wherever it can, so that the later stages of a port, which
keep that API, keep it passing. A test of a C form an item keeps, such as an unsafe
adoption, a function pointer's unsafe constructor, a trampoline or an export, goes with
the stage that removes the form.

How thoroughly a wrapper is tested follows how long it lasts. One a port will replace, a
type wrapped ahead of its port or a dependency whose module will be ported, keeps its safe
API through the port: it gets the tests of its public interface, which outlive it, and
none of its internals. A permanent one, every wrapper of a wrap campaign, the foundational
modules' and one whose later stage is held back for good, gets every kind.

The builds the tests run against and how coverage is measured are
[`testing-builds`](builds/SKILL.md)'s, and the gates every landing passes
[`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. UB tests

UB tests show that a workset's public API is free of UB.

The unsafe public interface is tested with one suite per public unsafe function or method
a workset adds, its inputs built through the safe API wherever one exists. A workset that
adds no public unsafe API has no UB tests on the unsafe interface.

The sanitizers available are those the campaign built: the instrumented variants of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`, where `asan-ubsan` provides ASan and UBSan, `msan` MSan, `tsan` TSan
and `bsan` BSan. A sanitizer without a variant is not available, so no test is written for
it and none runs under it. Miri needs no C build and is always available.

A target that ships its own sanitizers, because the standard ones cannot run against it,
is tested with those instead, each standing for the sanitizer it implements.

Each available sanitizer is a separate obligation of an item while it reaches C or unsafe
code; once it reaches neither, as a port's later stages bring about, Miri covers it alone:

- ASan/UBSan: bounds errors, use-after-free, use-after-return, invalid free, double free,
  pointer/alignment UB, and integer/division/shift UB.
- MSan: use of uninitialized memory, including branches and addresses computed from it,
  uninitialized bytes crossing the FFI boundary, and struct tails or buffers a foreign
  initializer left partly unwritten. Its build instruments every component, the standard
  library through `-Zbuild-std` included: memory written by uninstrumented code reads as
  uninitialized, so a partial build reports falsely.
- BSan: conflicting foreign writes and retained foreign pointers across Rust reborrows.
  These tests are written like the others. BSan is the slowest instrument and reports
  false positives at the foreign boundary, so it runs only as
  [`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions section describes.
- TSan: races reachable through safe APIs, including every asserted `Send` or `Sync`
  implementation and threaded callback.
- Miri: Rust-side lifetime, bounds, initialization, validity, alignment, intrinsic, and
  `repr` assumptions. Miri cannot call the foreign library, read its globals or spawn a
  process, so every test that cannot run under it carries
  `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore = "<reason>")]` on its test function, naming what stops it:
  `"calls C"`, `"reads a C global"`, and so on. A test is marked only after it was run
  alone under Miri and seen to stop there; never to silence a Miri report of undefined
  behaviour, a panic or a failed assertion, which are findings. The mark goes once what it
  names no longer stops the test, as a module's switch or a later stage brings about. Neither
  `#[cfg(not(miri))]` nor test-name filters stand in for the attribute: with it in place,
  Miri runs every other test.

A leak is not undefined behaviour, in Rust or in C, so neither a LeakSanitizer report,
which ASan's runtime makes by default, nor Miri's leak check is a UB candidate.

UB tests exercise every owner and borrowed form, shared and mutable access path, lifecycle
strategy, generic instance, and callback variant a batch emits. They attempt to outlive the
owner, alias a reborrow, reenter a callback, and drop a parent first. Storage that C and
Rust both allocate or free, or whose allocator a port moves, is tested for a free through
the wrong allocator.

When the type system should reject a program, the test is a compile-fail doctest or a
`trybuild` case.

## 2. Equivalence tests

Equivalence tests run the C and the Rust that translates it on independently owned inputs
built from one description, and compare:

- return values and errors;
- out-parameters and buffers;
- callbacks;
- state transitions; and
- lifecycle effects.

They use multi-call sequences and compare after each step; single calls are only a
baseline.

The C side of a test meets the preconditions the C sets its callers, as the wrapper meets
them before its own calls: a library's global initialisation, which writes state its
routines read without synchronisation, runs before the test's first call that reads it,
since the harness runs other tests beside it on other threads.

They compare what the C specifies, through the mapping the safe API applies to it, such as
its status returns as errors and its null pointers as absent values, and not what it leaves
unspecified, such as an iteration order, a message's text, a pointer's value or an
allocation count. A confirmed C defect is not copied into Rust. The divergence is
documented, equivalence tests are retained for the unaffected behaviour, and the
corrected-behaviour regression is a unit test.

`equiv_pub` holds the module's exported API to the C strictly. `equiv_priv` compares an
internal routine with its C counterpart only where one exists, since an idiomatic port may
restructure the internals; a C function the raw bindings do not reach, one with internal
linkage, is compared through the functions that call it. A macro that implements
logic is compared where it expands, through the functions that hold its expansions, since a
test of their callers compares the callers' logic, not the macro's. When no function the
raw bindings reach runs any of its expansions, directly or through the functions it calls,
no equivalence test compares it: its unit tests check it against the replacement list at
each expansion site's arguments, and the batch reports the sites as unreached, until the
port of the module that holds them compares them.

In a port, equivalence tests are the evidence of a module's migration. While its waves run,
the variants still build its C, which they reach through the raw bindings while the ported
Rust runs under its own names; at its switch they are retired with the C, and the
module evolves as Rust from then on, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes. Only its exports still keep the C contract, which the C tests that stay check.

## 3. Unit tests

A unit test is the right kind when Rust assertions supply the verdict: `unit_pub` on the
public interface, whose tests outlive the C, and `unit_priv` on internal facilities,
including:

- Rust-only `Iterator`, `Debug`, `Clone`, conversions, and builders;
- input rejected by Rust before FFI, including the error and no panic;
- deliberate correction of defective C behaviour;
- unsafe adoption through `from_raw`, `from_ptr`, or similar constructors;
- private or `pub(crate)` constructors and internal destructor/drop plumbing; and
- resource release exercised through any of those raw, unsafe, or internal paths.

## 4. C tests carried over

The `unit_pub` tests the port batches write for a module's items mirror the regression
cases of the C tests tied to it: their inputs, edge cases and call sequences, with the
assertions adapted to the safe Rust contract, so that what the C suites established
outlives them. Each names the C test case it carries over, so that before a C test
leaves, at the module's switch or with the exports it calls, the cases none carries
over are listed, and each is carried over or recorded as behaviour the safe API
deliberately changes. A `port/unexport` carries over every C test case that still references the
export it removes, whatever its subject, as a Rust test of that subject, reaching what is
still C through its wrappers, and removes the case from `c/`.

# Porting workflow

How a `port` campaign proceeds. It follows the [binding workflow](../binding-workflow/SKILL.md) throughout;
this document gives the principles a port follows and where it differs. How each item is
ported is [`porting`](../../rust/porting/SKILL.md).

## 1. Principles

### 1.1 Rust consumers

A port produces a Rust library for Rust-native applications. Its public API is the safe
Rust one; the installed C headers and the C ABI they describe are not kept for C
applications outside the target. The crate bundles the C that remains, as
[`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes, so that a consumer has the whole
library and reaches what is not ported yet through its raw bindings.

A ported module's C-facing surface is only what the target's own remaining C still
consumes, its translation units, tests and executables alike: its `extern "C"` exports,
under their bare C names, through which that C calls the Rust that replaced the module. The
remaining C depends on the Rust, never the Rust on a C copy of a ported module, so that
each function has one implementation and each global one copy. The surface shrinks as that
C is ported.

A type, public or internal, therefore keeps its C layout, and its `wrap`, only while
unported C of the target accesses that layout. The target's tests do not count, as
[Tests follow their modules](#12-tests-follow-their-modules) describes, and neither does a
definition in an installed header: the C consumers it would serve are outside the target.

### 1.2 Tests follow their modules

Each module carries the C tests tied to it, those whose subject it is, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Bundling section describes.
They assert the C contract, which a safe Rust implementation may change. Those that reach
the module's internals run while it is C and leave with it at its switch. Those that
use only its public API stay, and check its exports, which keep that contract for the C
that calls them, until their `port/unexport` carries them over, as the
[conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes. The tests its
port batches write mirror their regression cases, as
[`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s C tests carried over section describes. A
test's access to a module's internals is a use within that module, so it never keeps a type
wrapped.

A C test that only calls a module, to set up or tear down its fixtures, is not tied to it:
once the module has switched, the test reaches it through its exports, so that it checks
its own subject with the ported Rust under it, as part of the integration regression gate. A
test never keeps an export the remaining C no longer needs: the export's `port/unexport`
carries over the test cases that still reference it, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section describes.

A test whose subject is several modules is tied to each of them, and leaves at the first
point at which it would leave as a test of one of them alone. Each ported module's own
tests cover it from then on.

A test case whose body the configured build compiles empty, under a configuration the
target is built without, such as `GIT_WIN32`, tests nothing of the target: it is out of
scope, as a configured-out translation unit is, tied to no module and holding nothing back.

### 1.3 One language per module

A module is in one language at a time. The campaign maintains C and Rust side by side, but
on disjoint modules, never the same code in both.

While the waves of a module's `wrap` and `port` items run, its C is the reference its
ports are tested against, and the target is built and linked from C alone.
Once the last of them has landed, the module switches to Rust, once, as [Builds](#3-builds)
describes: the Rust module replaces the TU in the target's link, its C is removed from the
build and from the tree, and its tests switch with it. The removal is made on the working branch; the shipping branch keeps the C until
the user approves shipping the module. From then on the module is Rust's: what it still
keeps for the remaining C, its types' C layouts and storage and its exports, its later
stages remove after the switch, as [Later stages](#4-later-stages) describes.

The headers bundled with the module stay while remaining C includes them, declaring the
module's exports, its `static inline` functions included, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../rust/porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Static inline functions section describes, and go with the last C
file that includes them.

The module's equivalence tests, which need the C, are retired with it, and the behaviour
they established is kept by its unit tests. Before the module's equivalence tests are
retired, each that needs no C is carried over to the module's unit tests, where what it
compares with stays after the switch, such as the constants of a header that remaining C
still includes. The raw bindings of its
exported functions and globals then reach its exports, so that a consumer's raw calls keep
working, and an allowlist entry goes with the export it reaches. Those of its functions and
globals that have no export, which only its own C referenced, are removed with their
allowlist entries at the switch.

A ported module's items therefore reach the rest of its module natively from the start:
an edge within a module needs neither a `wrap` binding nor an export, only the edges that
leave it.

## 2. Batches

A port campaign's schedule mixes both kinds of batch, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s
Waves and batches section describes: a selected symbol is `port` from the start, a
selected type is `wrap` while another module's unported C depends on its layout and `port`
once none does, and a dependency outside the selected migration set stays `wrap`. A type
whose layout only its own module and tests use is `port` from the start. Each batch runs
the agent its objective names, in the same waves.

## 3. Builds

A module's waves do not change the compiled target. Its `port` batches add Rust that is
built and tested on its own, against the target's C build, which still compiles the
module's C and links no Rust: there is no build switch, and no batch flips one. The
module's `ffi_export` gateway is written with its items but compiled only under its export
feature, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports and Export features sections
describe, which stays off, so its bare-named exports never collide with the C the tests
link. Native Rust items carry mangled names and cannot collide with it.

The C stays until the switch: the target's other C still calls the module's symbols, which
only the exports could define, and the module's equivalence tests and its cut cycles still
run through it.

Once the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port` items has landed, it switches
in one step, with concurrent modules as part of its branch's integration into the working
branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Integration section
describes: its export feature is deleted, so that its gateway compiles from then on, its TU
and the C tests tied to it that reach its internals are removed from `c/`, and the
remaining C reaches the module through its exports. The C side of the
step is a commit on the fork's `main`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section
describes, and the campaign's commit records the submodule at it: integrations run one at a
time, so the two repositories move together.

The step's parts run in this order, both sides before the builds:

1. The Rust side, in one commit. The module's export feature is deleted, its equivalence
   tests are retired, those that need no C carried over first, the allowlist entries of its
   functions and globals that have no export are removed, and the bindings are regenerated
   against the builds in use, whose headers the switch does not change.
   Deleting the feature removes or rewrites every mention of its name in the crate, in its
   sources, its tests, its manifest and its build script, a `cfg_attr` or a `cfg(any(…))`
   as much as the gateway's attribute: an unknown `cfg`, or a lint expectation left unmet,
   fails the lints with warnings denied.
2. The C side: the module's TU and its tied C tests leave the fork.
3. The builds, from the C that remains. Each variant is configured, the Rust library is
   built, then the C is built and linked: the C that remains links the module's exports,
   which the Rust library holds only once the export feature is deleted.
4. The gates, over those builds.

From then on, the C that remains is linked in two ways, and no process holds a module both
as C and as Rust, nor its Rust twice:

- a Rust consumer, the campaign's own tests included, links the safe crate and the C that
  remains, which the crate bundles, statically or as shared libraries, as the raw bindings'
  Build modes describe; and
- the target's remaining C consumers, its C tests and executables, link the C that remains
  and the safe crate's Rust static library, built in campaign mode so that it carries no C
  of its own, through the target's actual build system.

The C tests that remain run over that second link as the integration regression gate, as
[`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes.
For that link, the first switch changes the fork's C build so that the remaining C's
tests and executables link the safe crate's Rust library, static or shared, in the build
system's own idiom, and each later switch takes its module's C out of that build.

## 4. Later stages

A module switches once. Its later-stage waves, `port/layout`, `port/memory` and
`port/unexport`, run after its switch, each once the switches its release point
waits for have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section times them: as the remaining C stops using its types' layouts and storage and
calling its exports, they nativize the types and remove the exports. They belong to no run
of the module and integrate nothing: each forks from the working branch and is promoted
back to it, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Lifecycle section
describes. A stage changes no C, since the C that held it back has left the build, but for
what still names the export a `port/unexport` removes. That
change is a commit on the fork's `main`, which the stage's commit records, as a switch's
is, and the stage's C tests run over variants built from the C it leaves, as
[Builds](#3-builds) describes for a switch.

## 5. Scope

The unit of a port is a module: its scope is whole modules, the foundational ones
included, which stay `wrap`, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational modules section
describes. Porting a few named items without their module is not described.

{

#if defined(GIT_THREADS)
# if defined(GIT_WIN32)
#  define GIT_MEMORY_BARRIER MemoryBarrier()
# elif defined(GIT_BUILTIN_ATOMIC)
#  define GIT_MEMORY_BARRIER __atomic_thread_fence(__ATOMIC_SEQ_CST)
# elif defined(GIT_BUILTIN_SYNC)
#  define GIT_MEMORY_BARRIER __sync_synchronize()
# endif
#else
# define GIT_MEMORY_BARRIER /* noop */
#endif
/* Thread-local data */
#if !defined(GIT_THREADS)
# define git_tlsdata_key int
#elif defined(GIT_WIN32)
# define git_tlsdata_key DWORD
#elif defined(_POSIX_THREADS)
# define git_tlsdata_key pthread_key_t
#else
# error unknown threading model
#endif
/**
 * Create a thread-local data key.  The destroy function will be
 * called upon thread exit.  On some platforms, it may be called
 * when all threads have deleted their keys.
 *
 * Note that the tlsdata functions do not set an error message on
 * failure; this is because the error handling in libgit2 is itself
 * handled by thread-local data storage.
 *
 * @param key the tlsdata key
 * @param destroy_fn function pointer called upon thread exit
 * @return 0 on success, non-zero on failure
 */
int git_tlsdata_init(git_tlsdata_key *key, void (GIT_SYSTEM_CALL *destroy_fn)(void *));
/**
 * Set a the thread-local value for the given key.
 *
 * @param key the tlsdata key to store data on
 * @param value the pointer to store
 * @return 0 on success, non-zero on failure
 */
int git_tlsdata_set(git_tlsdata_key key, void *value);
/**
 * Get the thread-local value for the given key.
 *
 * @param key the tlsdata key to retrieve the value of
 * @return the pointer stored with git_tlsdata_set
 */
void *git_tlsdata_get(git_tlsdata_key key);
/**
 * Delete the given thread-local key.
 *
 * @param key the tlsdata key to dispose
 * @return 0 on success, non-zero on failure
 */
int git_tlsdata_dispose(git_tlsdata_key key);
#endif

# Layout types whose state is written through shared access

Status: `open`.

## Signal

One representation written by hand (`evolution` §2), and a rule that forces a hand-written
layer `define_ctype!` could cover. `define_ctype!` lays a type out as its C struct alone,
`#[repr(transparent)] struct Foo(ffi::foo, PhantomData<…>)`. A value Rust holds hands out
its handles from `&self`, so they carry a pointer that may only be read through, as
`CRefSeam::as_ptr`'s documentation says. That is right for every C type whose writes go
through an exclusive handle. It is wrong for one whose state its holders change through
shared access, as an atomic counter's is: no write through a shared handle is sound over
a value Rust holds, and a `static` of such a type may be placed in read-only memory.

## Evidence

- `wave-226/batch-0/run-1`, `src/util/thread.c`, wraps `git_atomic32` and `git_atomic64`
  (`thread.h`): one `volatile int` or `int64_t` that libgit2's threads change only with
  `__atomic` builtins. Examples are every `git_refcount`, the runtime's `init_count`, and
  the object cache's `git_cache__current_storage`. The port batches that follow port
  `git_atomic32_inc` and its siblings over them, and the runtime's globals become Rust
  `static`s. Every write to these types goes through shared access.
- With `define_ctype!`, `Atomic32::new(0).as_ref().val().fetch_add(1, SeqCst)`, through
  `AtomicI32::from_ptr` on the projected field, is a write through a pointer derived from a
  shared borrow of a type with no `UnsafeCell`. That write is UB. `reproducer/`, beside this
  proposal, does it over ffibox `568bcb5`, and `cargo +nightly-2026-10-08 miri run` stops it:
  "Undefined Behavior: … only grants SharedReadOnly permission", the tag created by
  `define_ctype!`'s `as_ref`. So
  the run hand-wrote both layout types over `UnsafeCell<ffi::git_atomic32>`. It wrote one
  local `macro_rules!`, `atomic_type!` in `src/libgit2/src/util/thread.rs`, of about 140
  lines, which restates `define_ctype!`'s expansion: the layout type, both handles over
  `CBorrowedPtr`, `unsafe impl CCell`, the seams, and `as_ref` / `as_mut`. The only change
  is the `UnsafeCell`.
- `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s contract (ffibox `568bcb5`) lets nothing write the object while a
  shared handle lives, except through a `Mut` of the same borrow, or under a lock that
  every read through `Ref` takes. An atomic takes no lock. Each of its reads is atomic,
  and so is each concurrent write C makes. So the port's export of `git_atomic32_inc`
  adopts `a` as an `Atomic32Ref` while other C threads increment the same count. That keeps
  the atomics' own soundness argument, but not the trait's literal text. The record's row
  for `ffibox-ref-contract-self-locking` widened that text for a self-locking object; an
  object of atomics is the lock-free case of the same rule.
- G9's handle rule is "no Rust reference over foreign memory that anything may write
  while the reference lives". Read literally, it forbids the `&'a AtomicI32` the run's
  `val` accessor lends. The hazard G9 excludes is a reference that asserts what is false:
  immutability, or exclusive access. A shared reference to a standard atomic asserts
  neither. It asserts liveness, alignment, and that every concurrent access is atomic,
  which is the atomic's contract. The standard library offers `AtomicI32::from_ptr` for
  exactly this interoperation.

## Goal

Crustify's Safety goal (soundness), and ffibox's G1 (mirror standard Rust: a C atomic
field's safe form is the standard atomic) and G12 (obligations local: the contract an
atomics wrapper relies on is stated by the trait it implements, not argued against it).
The fitness measure: the hand-written `unsafe impl CCell` count in the campaign's crate,
which this run raised by two. No `ub` or `contracts` finding should appear on a layout
type written through shared access.

## Destination

ffibox: `define_ctype!` (`src/macros.rs`), `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s and `CRefSeam::as_ptr`'s
contracts (`src/traits.rs`), `docs/borrows.md`'s conventions, `docs/hand-written.md`'s
scope, and G9's handle row in `docs/goals.md`. Once that lands, `binding-types`' Field accessors
section gains the case's line: a field C changes through shared access, with atomic
operations alone, is lent by the shared handle as the standard atomic of its width, and its
layout type is declared `interior`.

## Change

1. `define_ctype!` takes an option, `interior`, for a C type whose state its holders write
   through shared access. It lays the type out as
   `#[repr(transparent)] struct Foo(UnsafeCell<ffi::foo>, PhantomData<…>)`. Its `as_ref`
   then hands out a pointer that may be written through, as `UnsafeCell::get`'s does, and a
   `static` of it is writable. All else is unchanged: `CCell`, the handles and the seams.
   The layout type stays `!Sync` until the binding asserts `Sync`.
2. `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s contract admits a third kind of concurrent write. Beside writes
   through a `Mut` of the same borrow, and writes under a lock every read through `Ref`
   takes, it admits writes made atomically to bytes that every access through `Ref` makes
   atomically, of the same size. `CRefSeam::as_ptr`'s note extends to such a type: one

modules (`utf8.c`, `opt.c`, `api.c`, `http.c`), one later stage (wave 232) and two header modules;
the variants' current generation is `crustify/builds.gen5`, and the fork's local `fork/main` is at
`230c9dbdb`, five commits past the fork's published `main`.

### `libgit2/src/util/thread.c` wave 226 batch 0: the module's types

A `wrap` batch of the module's three types, ahead of the three `port` batches of its symbols on
the same wave branch. `st::git_atomic32` and `st::git_atomic64` are `Atomic32` and `Atomic64`,
and `tdf::git_atomic_ssize` is the alias `AtomicSsize`, of `Atomic64` where pointers are 64 bits
wide. Their one field, `val`, is lent through each shared handle as the standard atomic it is
(`val() -> &'a AtomicI32` / `&'a AtomicI64`), which is what the ports of `git_atomic32_inc` and
its siblings build on. C writes it only with sequentially consistent `__atomic` builtins. It
also reads it plainly in `smart.c`, `smart_protocol.c` and `settings.c`, a C race the binding
cannot touch. The layout types are written by hand over `UnsafeCell<git_atomic32>`, with their
handles and seams, through a local `atomic_type!` macro. A `define_ctype!` value hands out a
pointer that may only be read through, so an atomic write through a handle of a value Rust
holds is UB (Miri: `SharedReadOnly`). A `static` of either type is writable, as the runtime's
globals will need. Both types and their handles are `Send` and `Sync` (`Send/Sync` `+12`). They
need no lifecycle: zeroed storage is the value 0, and nothing releases it.

`st::git_thread` is `Thread`, a `define_ctype!` layout, `CZeroable`, neither `Clone` nor `Send`.
`fld::git_thread.thread` is read as std's `RawPthread` and written by the batch's one public
`unsafe fn`, `ThreadMut::set_thread`. Its contract carries what a later join through the object
follows. That is the boundary scan's only site in the changeset: no safe form stores an
arbitrary id, and one that owns a `JoinHandle` is `git_thread_create`'s port's to design. The
`pthread_t` the bindings add is the same type as std's `RawPthread`, a compile-time check; libc's
wrapper binds no `pthread_t`. The three types' findings are in the ownership store. They have no
pointer field, and their lifecycle routines are the `git_thread_*` macros, which take none.

The raw bindings gain the three types and `git_atomic_ssize` in `allowlist.txt` (`+41` lines of
`bindings.rs`, which `+LoC` leaves out). Tests: 10 `unit_pub`, 5 `ub_safe` (shared and lent
atomics, a `static` and a compare-and-swap loop from four threads, an exclusive handle sent to a
thread), 4 `ub_unsafe` (`set_thread` within its contract: live threads' ids still owned by their
`JoinHandle`s, ids naming no thread, replacement, an array of objects), 5 compile-fail cases
(`thread_handles_not_send` split under `toolchain/`, since its notes quote `core`'s
`PhantomData`), and 4 doctests, 2 of them compile-fail. No test calls C, so no equivalence test
was written. The C over these layouts is the port batches' functions, and bindgen's layout
assertions and the module's `const` assertions compare the layouts. The 19 tests pass plain,
under ASan+UBSan and TSan, under Miri (the doctests too) and under BSan, each alone. The module's
and its 38 dependents' tests pass plain and under ASan+UBSan, 1,395 of them. The package (703
files) builds alone in bundled mode, as `package-gate-procedure` has it, with the workspace's Git
patch of ffibox. Its `lib` tests were not run, since the module has none.

6:# Binding symbols
12:## 1. Functions
61:## 2. Globals

171:## 5. Lifecycle strategies
## 4. Macros

A C macro is bound to a Rust form of its own:

- a type-generating macro, to one generic type, through [`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md),
  its instances aliases of it;
- a constant macro, to a `const`, defined from its generated binding;
- a symbol alias, through the safe wrapper of the symbol it names, each of whose stand-ins
  stands in for the alias too and carries its anchor beside the symbol's own: where the
  symbol is a lifecycle primitive, the strategy methods that call it, as
  [Lifecycle strategies](#5-lifecycle-strategies) describes; and
- a macro that implements logic, to a function, `#[inline]`, or `const` where its body
  computes on its arguments alone, which reimplements the body and reaches C only for the
  symbols its expansion uses, through their safe wrappers, and for the fields it accesses,
  through their accessors. A `macro_rules!` takes its place only where a function cannot
  express it: control flow that leaves its caller, token pasting or stringification, an
  argument used as a place, or one evaluated lazily or more than once. One evaluated
  more than once calls for a `macro_rules!` only where a caller depends on it: where every expansion site
  passes an argument without side effects, whose result is the same evaluated once, the
  macro is a function, its documentation naming the difference, as a `MIN` or `MAX` of the
  usual form is.

A macro whose expansion depends on the build's configuration, which the Rust does not see,
is the exception: it is reached through a shim, `crustify_<NAME>`, bound and wrapped.

## 5. Lifecycle strategies

10-item's analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes. A type takes the type
11-route, for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`binding-types`](types/SKILL.md)
12-describes; a symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, macros and
13-lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

16-
17-Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.
18-
19-Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:
20-
21-- wrapped-layout projection;
22-- wrapped FFI calls; and
23-- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.
24-
25-They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
26-Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
27-each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
28-invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
29-guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
30-change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
31-public ones whose obligation no type expresses.
32-
33-The obligation of an `unsafe fn` that stores a value C keeps, such as a pointer a later
34-call follows, lasts as long as C holds it, in the object or in any copy C makes of it: until
35-a setter replaces it or a call clears it, the contract naming which, or else as long as its
36-holders live. It is never bounded by the calls that use the value, since safe code makes
37-those after the `unsafe` call has returned.
38-
39-A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
40-[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
41-carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
42-binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
43-composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
44-C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
45-kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
46-while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
47-on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
48-Equivalence tests section describes.
49-
50-A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
51-wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
52-the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
53-ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
54-ports. Every unsafe block carries
55-the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.

An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust
standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust,
or crosses to C only as values the boundary converts: `errno` set from an `io::Error` by
an export gateway, a `struct stat` filled from an `fs::Metadata`. It is reached through the
library's bindings wherever that state is shared with C: a lock, a handle or an allocation
the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a
library's `decision` adopts or overrides; the first batch that needs the entity checks that
route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not
hold, and reports which in its final message, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section describes. An
entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.

content.content:
## 1. Routes

What a campaign uses of an out-of-tree library is reached, in this order of preference:

1. through the Rust standard library, wherever no state is shared with C, as
   [Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) describes;
2. through established crates adopted for parts of the library, extended in a fork where
   they lack a little, as [Adopted crates](#6-adopted-crates) describes;
3. bound locally, in the consuming module's own `ffi_import` region over the library's
   established `-sys` crate, such as `libc`, for what is left too small to be worth a
   wrapper, as [Local bindings](#7-local-bindings) describes; and
4. through the library's crustify campaign, a wrap campaign of its own whose crate is the
   library's Crustify wrapper, as the rest of this section and
   [Side campaigns](#3-side-campaigns) describe.

## 6. Adopted crates

A crate is adopted for a coherent part of what the campaign uses of a library, the
entities a subsystem, a header's API or a kind of resource (sockets, memory maps,
processes) groups, never for an item or two: entities that share state, such as a stream's
initializer, its operations and its finalizer, take the same crate. A library may be
covered by several crates, the fewest that cover what the campaign uses: libc's uses may
be the standard library's for files and threads, one crate's for sockets and another's for
the remaining system calls. What no adopted crate covers takes the next route.

Each entity's `matches` record what each candidate offers for it, and how closely; each
candidate's `quality_assessment` weighs it, in prose, on the considerations below. Only
soundness and advisories are gates: a crate with undefined behaviour reachable from its
safe API, or with an unfixed advisory on what the campaign uses, is not adopted unless a
fork fixes it. The others are weighed against the alternative routes, which are never free:
a crustify campaign or local bindings put the campaign's own unsafe code where the crate
would have put none.

- **coverage**: it serves what the campaign uses of those entities, as their `matches`
  show. Same behaviour is not required: a port is a new implementation, and a difference
  the port can absorb in its own safe code (a verifier, a loop in place of a sizing call,
  configuration loaded eagerly), or that it can adopt deliberately and record as the safe
  API's changed behaviour (an option it rejects, a deprecated fallback it drops), weighs
  against the crate only by its cost. What only an extension of the crate would provide
  is extended, as below;
- **shared state**: where the remaining C shares an entity's state with the Rust, such as
  a handle the C still uses, the crate exposes that state to C, which the entity's match
  note says, citing the release point after which the C stops sharing it. A crate that
  binds the C library and exposes its raw handles can; one that reimplements the library
  serves only where no state crosses to the remaining C, as
  [Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) describes. An entity
  only one module uses, whose port keeps the state in Rust, shares none;
- **soundness** (a gate): a read of its public API and its unsafe code finds no undefined
  behaviour reachable from its safe API, by the hazards
  [`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary excludes from the campaign's
  own; a deterministic scan of its unsafe surface backs the judgement where that surface
  is large or the judgement is borderline;
- **advisories** (a gate): no unfixed security advisory affects the version and the
  features the campaign uses; and
- **maintenance**: how likely the crate is to keep up with its dependencies, toolchains and
  advisories: its release history and its maintainers, weighed by how much the crate does
  and how settled its scope is, since a complete crate with a narrow scope needs few
  releases. A crate whose `-sys` crate the alternative route would use anyway is no
  riskier than that route. Its license and minimum Rust version suit the campaign's.

recommended for the entities it serves best. Once the user adopts it,
those entities get no wrapper and no batches: their consumers use the crate directly, and
their bindings name its types and functions where they would name the wrapper's.

A crate that lacks a little of what it is adopted for is extended rather than passed over: in a fork
cloned beside the campaign's repository, as a wrapper is, on a branch of its own, which the
campaign's workspace pins with a Cargo `[patch]`. The extension is offered upstream, as a
pull request opened with the user's approval, so that the fork can be dropped once it is
merged.

first campaign that meets one. -->

What a library's adopted crates leave uncovered, when it is too small to be worth a
wrapper, a few functions, is bound where it is used: over the library's established `-sys` crate, in
the consuming module's `ffi_import` region, behind a safe API of that module's, as
[`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md) describes for any item, by the batch that consumes
it. What grows past a few functions, or what several modules need, is the library's
crustify campaign's.

## 8. Confirmation

An entity's route is a recommendation made before any of its uses was translated. The first
batch that binds or ports one of its users checks the route against the code it translates,
by the uses the entity's `match` and note describe, and reports what it found in its final
message, which is recorded as the entity's `confirmation`. Each later batch takes
the confirmed route.

When the route does not hold, the batch reaches the entity through another route the
library's `decision` already allows, in this order: the standard library, where
[Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) allows it; another crate the
decision adopts for the library; the decision's `uncovered` route. A `crustify-campaign`
route that the library's crustify campaign does not yet cover is reported, and advanced as
[Side campaigns](#3-side-campaigns) describes, before the batch runs again. Where no route
the decision allows serves the entity, because the library leaves nothing `uncovered` or
only a crate the user has not adopted would, the batch reports it, and it is put
to the user, whose answer is recorded among the decision's `overrides`.

---
name: ffimap
description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB, and, as a hint only, when planning an audit's scope and worksets."
---

# ffimap

ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.

It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```

Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \
    --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \
    > <file>.json
```

Raw bindings that are a module of the crate, not a crate of their own, laid out and
generated as [`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes, are named to `--sys-crates`
by their path, `crate::<path>`, beside the `-sys` crates that remain. A named module joins
the inventory and leaves every other counter, as a `-sys` crate does. Left unnamed, its C
types and functions are in no inventory, the cells that read it are taken over the other
crates' alone, and the generated code counts as the crate's own, all with no error. A module
that holds hand-written code beside its declarations is left unnamed, since naming it would
take that code out of the scan.

In a port campaign, a scan names with `--features` the export feature of every module not
yet switched, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Export features section
names them, so that the `ffi_export` gateways compiled under them are counted. Every scan
names the module's unsafe regions, as the conventions' Unsafe regions section names them,
with `--regions`.

Two scans are compared only when they name the same seams, regions and features.

Its counters form one tree, each named by its dotted path into the scan's `counts`, as
ffimap's `docs/schema.md` describes; a metric is a counter, or a combination of counters
that schema allows: a partition's leaves summed, a share read against the record it cuts,
or subtracted from it. `--sites <counter> ...` also lists where each named counter's
increments are, and takes leaves only, such as `fn.unsafe.pub`; the workspace is named
before it. The counters that recur:

- `fn.unsafe.pub`, the public `unsafe fn`s, the crate's public unsafe surface, of which
  `fn.unsafe.of_which.other.pub` are those neither a trait nor a seam required; and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, the raw pointers in
  their signatures;
- `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`, the
  raw pointers in public fields and in the signatures of public safe fns, together
  `raw_ptr.total.safe.pub`, the raw pointers on the safe public interface; and their
  `of_which.void` shares, the type-erased ones among them;
- `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, the references to a cell, less their
  `of_which.self_in_ref_accessor` and `of_which.self_in_trait_impl` shares, the positions
  ffibox sanctions: references to C memory where a handle belongs, which assert `noalias`,
  `readonly` or validity over memory C may write; `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std`, the same
  of the raw C structs; and `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`, the borrows,
  slices and strings formed from a raw pointer, over bytes C must neither free nor change
  while they live;
- `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`,
  each an unchecked assertion that a value may move to or be shared with another thread;
- `raw_ptr.deref.wr` and `raw_ptr.deref.rd`, raw-pointer writes and reads, each a pointer
  the implementer vouches is non-null, aligned, live, initialized and unaliased by a live
  reference; and
- `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}` and
  `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`, the types that hold a raw pointer and
  tear it down or copy it by hand, and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none.{pub,priv}`, those
  that declare nothing about it. Each of these five also has a `.total`, the sum of its two
  leaves, which is no leaf for `--sites`.

ffimap is neither complete nor sound: its sites are where review starts, not all it
covers. It does not count the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, such as a reference
or lifetime-annotated handle made from a raw pointer by `&*p`, `from_ptr`, `from_raw` or
`from_raw_parts`, or changed by a `transmute`: those are found in the source.

What follows is how ffimap serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffimap adds there.

## Binding and porting

### Binding › Safe boundary

Before a batch lands, a scan with `--sites fn.unsafe.pub raw_ptr.field.pub
raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub` lists the public
`unsafe fn`s and the raw pointers on the safe public interface, and each of those sites
that belongs to the batch's changeset and that a safe variant could replace is fixed.
Its `--sites` also name the unsafe code outside both regions,
`code.unsafe_block.of_which.outside_regions`, another crate's macro expansions included,
which the `unsafe_code` lint misses, and `fn.unsafe.of_which.outside_regions.pub` and
`.priv`: outside the raw bindings, each of those sites in the batch's changeset is moved
into its region.

## Accounting

### Accounting › Landing cells

A batch's row in the dashboard's `Batches: safety audit` table is the change in each of
the Safety audit's metrics, from a scan of the tip its landing rebased onto to a scan of
the tree it lands.

### Accounting › API stability

`ffimap api` measures a safe crate's consumer-facing API per C item, from rustdoc JSON, as
its `docs/api.md` describes, read in full before its first use. A C item is the
`<kind>::<path>` of a `Wraps` or `Replaces` anchor, its surface every stand-in the anchor
names and the handles and owners tied to it, each judged by the contract
[`binding-types`](../../rust/binding/types/SKILL.md)' Safe layout section gives a consumer:
the methods every form offers, its reborrows and dereferences, and the traits a consumer
can use, never a form's raw access or seams. A batch generates the safe crate's rustdoc
JSON on the tip its landing rebased onto and on the tree it lands, with a nightly whose
`format_version` the tool supports, and ffibox's, with private items, for the contracts of
the forms it defines:

```bash
cargo +<nightly> rustdoc -p <crate> --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json
ffimap api diff <base>.json <tree>.json --dep <ffibox>.json --items "<the worklist's keys>" --format json
```

Each item comes out `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed` or `new`, with its anchor's
move from `Wraps` to `Replaces` where a port made it. The batch's row in the dashboard's
`Batches: API stability` table counts them over its worklist, and over the crate's
unattributed public items, compared per module.

### Accounting › Records

An unseeded scan of the unsafe and FFI surface is recorded at each batch's, wave's and
the campaign's end, as `ffimap.json` in its artifact directory: a batch's in the run dir
of the run that landed it, a wave's in its wave's dir, as `layout` spells it, and the
campaign's in `crustify/artifacts/`. A module's end is the scan of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

A review locates the sites of its objectives with a scan, `--sites` with their counters,
and keeps those in its workset: the code its commits add or change, or its modules and
the types, trait impls and functions they name. The sites are where the reading starts,
as [`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s Worklists section describes; an
audit's review is the same review with no scan at all.

- `unsafety`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`.
- `contracts`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, whose `# Safety` obligations are evaluated.
- `ub`: these smells first, in this order:
  1. references into C memory: the references to a cell outside its sanctioned positions,
     `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}` less those shares, and to a raw C
     struct, `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, then
     `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`;
  2. thread-safety claims, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and
     `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`, checked against
     the C library's contract: a data race is reachable from safe code when the library
     does not allow what they assert;
  3. the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, found in the source: unsound when the
     handle can outlive the owner of the memory or the point at which C frees or
     invalidates it;
  4. raw pointers a consumer can set, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
     `raw_ptr.field.pub`, with their `of_which.void` shares: unsound when a safe path
     dereferences or frees what the consumer passed or stored;
  5. raw-pointer dereferences, `raw_ptr.deref.wr` then `raw_ptr.deref.rd`: first in the
     modules that also hold references into C memory, where a write may invalidate a
     reference, and outside a type's accessors; and
  6. hand-written teardown and copies, `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}`
     and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`.

## Audit

### Audit workflow › Scope and priority

In an audit a scan is a hint. Where the settings' `tool-hints` answer allows one, it is
run once each build configuration is in place, with `--sites` over the counters of the
audit's objectives, and set beside the reading of the crate: a site the reading missed is
read, and a module the scan reports nothing in is planned and reviewed from its source
like any other. A scan decides neither what is in scope nor its order, and no workset is
dropped, deferred or reviewed more lightly for having no sites.

A scan that fails, that covers part of the crate, such as the files of one configuration,
or that the source contradicts stops nothing: the plan stands on the reading, and the
failure is proposed as ffimap's defect.

### Audit workflow › Worksets

A site of `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop`, `.impl_clone`,
`ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send` or `.sync`, at either leaf, is a trait impl, named
`Drop for <type>`, `Clone for <type>`, `Send for <type>` or `Sync for <type>`. A review
that scans does so over its own modules, so the sites are not passed on.

### Audit workflow › Scope and priority

In an audit a scan is a hint. Where the settings' `tool-hints` answer allows one, it is
run once each build configuration is in place, with `--sites` over the counters of the
audit's objectives, and set beside the reading of the crate: a site the reading missed is
read, and a module the scan reports nothing in is planned and reviewed from its source
like any other. A scan decides neither what is in scope nor its order, and no workset is
dropped, deferred or reviewed more lightly for having no sites.

A scan that fails, that covers part of the crate, such as the files of one configuration,
or that the source contradicts stops nothing: the plan stands on the reading, and the
failure is proposed as ffimap's defect.

### Audit workflow › Worksets

A site of `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop`, `.impl_clone`,
`ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send` or `.sync`, at either leaf, is a trait impl, named
`Drop for <type>`, `Clone for <type>`, `Send for <type>` or `Sync for <type>`. A review
that scans does so over its own modules, so the sites are not passed on.

### `libgit2/src/util/utf8.c` wave 229 batch 0: the module's `port`

The module's whole `port`, the items of waves 229 to 231 folded into one batch, since each
depends on the one before: `glb::utf8proc_utf8class`, `fn::utf8_charlen`,
`fn::git_utf8_iterate`, `fn::git_utf8_char_length` and `fn::git_utf8_valid_buf_length`, in
`src/libgit2/src/util/utf8.rs`. The table is a `static` built by a `const fn` from its lead
byte ranges, which a `unit_priv` test checks against C's literal; `utf8_charlen` is the
private `sequence_len(&[u8]) -> Option<usize>`; the three functions are the native
`decode_char(&[u8]) -> Result<(char, usize), InvalidCodePoint>`, `char_count(&[u8]) -> usize`
and `valid_prefix_len(&[u8]) -> usize`. What `git_utf8_iterate` accepts is always a scalar
value, so the code point is a `char`. One C defect is not carried over: with `str_len` 0,
`utf8_charlen` skips its bound check and `git_utf8_iterate` reads past the size it is given;
no caller passes 0 (`next_hfs_char` loops while `*len`), and the port and its export refuse
empty bytes (-1, `*out` 0), documented on both and kept by a unit test. No out-of-tree
entity is used.

The crate's first `ffi_export` gateway, under the crate's first export feature,
`ffi-export-src-util-utf8-c`, declared off in `Cargo.toml`: `git_utf8_iterate`,
`git_utf8_char_length` and `git_utf8_valid_buf_length`, under their C names, for
`path.c`'s `next_hfs_char`, `diff_xdiff.c`'s `git_xdiff_cb` and, on Windows, `fs_path.c`,
whose `port/unexport` stages are waves 232, 860 and 1531. Each body runs in ffibox's
`barrier`, a panic reported as -1 by `git_utf8_iterate` and aborting the two that cannot
fail, and each export is checked against its raw binding by a constant, `[sys::<name>,
<name>]`, whose function items coerce to one pointer type only where the signatures agree:
`str_len: u32` in an export fails to build (`E0308`). The three functions were allowlisted
(`wrapper.h` gains `utf8.h`) for that check and the equivalence tests. As a scratch check,
not a gate, the feature on links the exports in place of the archive's `utf8.o` (no
`utf8proc_utf8class` in the binary, C's `next_hfs_char` resolving to Rust): the six `equiv`
tests then compare the gateway with the native API and pass, and so do the tests of
`path.c` and `diff_xdiff.c`. The pointer findings of the four functions are submitted to
the ownership store.

Tests: four `unit_priv` tests (the table against C's, empty bytes, every lead byte's class,
broken continuations), eleven `unit_pub` tests, three doctests and six `equiv` tests (the
cases of `test_utf8__char_length` and the boundaries, every lead byte followed by every kind
of byte, every byte pair, every three-byte sequence, every `char`'s encoding and the
four-byte forms past U+10FFFF, and walks that compare after each step).
`char_count_carries_over_the_c_test` carries over the module's one C test case,
`test_utf8__char_length`, unchanged.

Coverage: `run.sh` on a `git archive` of the wave tip `2216b0cd0` and on this tree, read
with `report.py` from each scratch tree's `src/libgit2` (`coverage-report-relative-rows`),
the unit column merging `lib` and `unit_pub`. Worklist: Rust `utf8.rs` 58 of 59 lines, 83 of
84 regions and 14 of 14 functions, the one line `decode_char`'s `_` arm, which no length
`sequence_len` returns reaches; the gateway is compiled out. C `utf8.c` 69 of 71 lines, 54
of 55 regions and 4 of 4 functions under `equiv` (40 of 71 at the tip), the two lines
`git_utf8_iterate`'s unreachable `default: return -1`; its own C test reaches
`git_utf8_char_length` alone. The tree was measured twice, the second after a test was made
to call the table's `const fn` at run time, which coverage did not count when only the
compiler evaluated it; the C total moved `45.02`% to `44.97`% between the two runs with the
C unchanged, run-to-run variation, as are the `ub_safe` and `ub_unsafe` C shifts, which this
batch's tests do not run. The Overview's Rust LoC moves by ffimap's `code.loc.total`
(`+132`) and `code.tests.loc.total` (`+357`). `+LoC` leaves out the regenerated
`bindings.rs` (`+41`), as earlier rows do. The `loc` cell is wavefront's `query dag --loc`.

The safety audit scans (ffimap `9aa2ef1`, flags as wave 225's) name the export feature on
this tree, the only one not yet switched, and none on the tip, which declares none: `raw→std`
`+1` is the gateway's `slice::from_raw_parts`, and `unsafe blocks` `+1` its `bytes` helper,
the exports' four blocks being `ffi_export`'s. The boundary scan's sites hold none in the
changeset. `ffimap api` over the worklist: the three exported functions `new`; the table
### Reading the batch tables

Batch rows from every sub-campaign share one table per route; the `module` cell names the
row's sub-campaign as `<link-unit>/<module>`, the same name as its Overview row.
Every type row is a `wrap` batch: the rows the wrap campaign landed, kept in the `Types`
tables' `objective` column since the template merged its wrap and port tables. A `wavefront` report category, for ownership findings the review resubmitted, is
counted under `+misc`.

Each batch is measured on two tree states: just before its first landing commit (the wave
base or the previous batch's landing) and its last landing commit. `cov (C/Rust)` is the
latter, from one instrumented build per state: the four workloads (`--lib` unit tests,
`ub_safe`, `ub_unsafe`, `equiv`) each run alone into their own profile directory against
the `coverage` prebuild, and their union is the cell. C is lcov line coverage over the 196
translation units `libgit2.so` links, with a zero baseline from the `.gcno` files so that
untouched TUs count; Rust is cargo-llvm-cov line coverage over `crustify/rust/libgit2`'s
non-`tests/` sources, minus every line inside a `#[cfg(test)]` item (the inline unit-test
modules). All workloads share one denominator, and the union is the union of their covered
lines. Every Rust cell and Rust delta in these tables was restated on 2026-10-12. The
earlier figures counted those test lines, 60% of the instrumented lines at the
`libgit2/index` tip, which held the integration suites' coverage far down and credited
the unit tests for running themselves. All 182 recorded states were re-measured; the C
cells and C deltas stay as first recorded. The eight `libgit2/config` states between
`beeda6a07` and the export revert `c5440d3ee` call the two reverted constructors, so they
were measured against a private coverage build of their own source, which exports them. A Σ `cov` cell is the state after the table's chronologically
last landing. The `(+C/+Rust pp)` pairs in the `…: tests` tables are each workload's own
coverage after minus before, so a batch that adds code its workload does not reach shows a
negative Rust delta. The safety audit deltas are the Safety audit's metrics over the same two
states, from the scans the `ffimap` skill names; the tables hold no row from before the
metrics were redefined, as `Safety audit metrics from ffimap's counter tree` describes.

Test counts are `#[test]` functions the landing commits add, by directory; trybuild
`compile_fail` cases are not counted. `+LoC` and `rv loc` count `.rs` lines under
`crustify/rust/`, so review reproducer crates under `crustify/reviews/` are excluded. The
measurement scripts live outside the repository, beside the orchestrator's other helpers;
each batch's `ffimap.json` beside it is the unseeded scan of its last landing commit.

#!/bin/bash
# Run cargo against one crustify prebuild of libgit2, instrumenting Rust to match.
#
#   crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]
#
# <variant> is a `variants` key of crustify/artifacts/build.json: plain, coverage, asan-ubsan,
# tsan or bsan. Each variant uses its own target dir under target/.
# The safe crate's build script, in campaign mode, links the variant's static archive (its
# `static` in build.json) into each test binary, so the C runs under the instrumentation the
# Rust is built with here, one runtime serving both. Set CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR to a private build
# of the variant, which carries the same archive, to link it instead of the shared one.
set -euo pipefail
variant=${1:?usage: cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]}
shift
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$here/target/$variant}
# pcre2-sys links the variant's side-campaign PCRE2, the one libgit2's C links, rather than
# building its vendored copy, which would shadow it in every test binary. The side campaigns'
# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done
case $variant in
  plain)
    exec cargo "$@" ;;
  coverage)
    # Source-based coverage on the pinned nightly, against the variant's clang-instrumented C,
    # which each test binary links statically, so that rustc's profiler runtime counts both;
    # crustify/scripts/coverage/ measures the suites as the testing spec's Coverage section does.
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/profraw/%p-%m.profraw}
