# API stability per C item `ffimap api` measures a promise a C-to-Rust migration makes to its Rust consumers: once a C item has a safe Rust API, wrapping it, porting it and its later stages leave that API alone. It reads the crate's rustdoc JSON, finds the Rust items that stand in for each C item through their anchors, and records their consumer-facing surface twice: raw, as the signatures stand, and as the **contract** a consumer may rely on whatever form a handle or an owner takes. Two such records, one at the item's first landing and one after a later landing, say whether the contract was kept, extended or changed. This document is what the two documents hold and every rule behind them. The scan's counters are [`schema.md`](schema.md)'s and have nothing to do with it. ## 1. Input ```sh cargo +nightly-2026-10-07 rustdoc -p CRATE --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json (cd ffibox && cargo +nightly-2026-10-07 rustdoc --lib -- -Z unstable-options \ --output-format json --document-private-items) ffimap api extract target/doc/CRATE.json --dep ffibox/target/doc/ffibox.json > before.json ``` `--dep` gives the rustdoc JSON of a crate the measured one depends on, and is repeatable. The contracts of handles and owners that are aliases into ffibox (`CBox`, `CArc`, `CVal`, …) need ffibox's, since the reborrows and trait impls those forms inherit live there; it is made with `--document-private-items` because the bounds rustdoc synthesises for ffibox's auto-trait impls name its private fields' types. Without it those contracts are unresolved, as section 6 describes. The measure is pure Python over the JSON. It does not use the driver, so the crate need not build on the driver's nightly, only document on one whose JSON format it reads. Rustdoc's JSON is unstable: each nightly writes a `format_version`, and the shape moves with it. `ffimap api` reads **format 61**, which nightly-2026-10-07 (the driver's pin) and nightly-2026-10-08 emit, and refuses any other with an error naming the version it found. Support for a new format is added by checking the fields `src/ffimap/rustdoc.py` reads against it and adding it to `FORMAT_VERSIONS`. ## 2. C items and their stand-ins A C item is keyed by its anchor's `::`: `fn::git_mailmap_new`, `st::git_mailmap`, `fld::git_buf.ptr`. An anchor is a doc-comment line of its own, exactly ``Wraps `::` `` or ``Replaces `::` ``, where the path is names separated by dots and a `fld` path names a member. Every public item of the crate that carries one is a **stand-in** of that C item, and an item carrying several (the accessor of two members) is a stand-in of each. What the extract reports about the anchors themselves, under `anchors`: - `malformed`: a line that tries to be an anchor and is not one -- the verb and a `kind::` path inside a sentence, with a trailing period, without backticks, or with a path that is not names. It keys nothing. - `unknown_kinds`: anchors whose kind is not one of the convention's (`fn`, `st`, `un`, `enm`, `fnp`, `tdf`, `fld`, `glb`, `mac`), counted by kind. They are keyed as written. - `without_alias`: anchors on an item with no `#[doc(alias)]` naming the anchor's path. An item whose own name is the anchor's path is left out: rustdoc rejects an alias equal to its item's name, and the name already answers a search for it. ## 3. Locators and paths Each stand-in is named by a **locator**, which is how one landing's record is matched with the next's: | item | locator | |---|---| | a free item | its canonical path | | an item of an inherent impl | `Ty::name` | | an item of a trait impl | `>::name` | | a trait's item, a variant, a field | its owner's locator `::name` | Lifetime names in a locator are erased to `'_`. A **canonical path** is the path a consumer names an item by. For an item of the crate it is the path rustdoc's `paths` table gives its definition when that path is public, else the shortest public path it is re-exported at, the first in order among equals. An item defined in a private module and re-exported from its parent is named by the parent's path, and a port that moves the definition into the parent changes nothing. An item of another crate is named by its definition's path in the `paths` table, `ffibox::refs::CBox` for instance, because this document does not record that crate's re-exports. Every type in a signature is rendered by its canonical path, never by what the source wrote, so an import or a reordering of the source gives the same bytes. A record's `paths` lists every public path the item is reached by, from the crate root through public modules and `pub use`, globs included. An associated item's are its owner's paths with its name appended. ## 4. Signatures Each stand-in's `sig` is normalised text by kind: - **functions and methods**: `decl` holds `const`, `async`, `unsafe`, the ABI, generics, the receiver (`self`, `&self`, `&'a mut self`, `self: Box`), the parameter types and return type, and where-clauses. A method also has the `impl` header it is declared in, generics and trait included, and a trait's method has `default`, whether it has a body. Parameter names are left out. - **structs, enums and unions**: `decl` holds the generics, the shape (`;`, `(n)`, `{}`) and `#[non_exhaustive]`. `fields` maps each public field to its type, and `variants` each variant to its shape and discriminant. `stripped` says whether rustdoc hid private fields or variants. `impls` maps the header of every trait impl rustdoc records for the type to its items (those it defines and the trait's provided ones it inherits) and its associated types and constants; the auto-trait impls rustdoc synthesises (`Send`, `Sync`, `Unpin`, `UnwindSafe`, `RefUnwindSafe`, and `Freeze` and `UnsafeUnpin` where the nightly records them), negative ones as `!Send`, are included, and blanket impls are not, since they follow from the type's other impls. `members` holds the items of its inherent impls that stand in for no C item, each with its impl header. - **traits**: `decl` with generics, supertraits and `unsafe`; `required` and `provided` items, each with its declaration; `dyn_compatible`. - **type aliases**: `decl` holds the whole target, `type = ffibox::refs::CBox<…>`. - **constants and statics**: type and value; **associated constants and types**: their declaration and, in an impl, its header; **variants** and **fields**: their shape or type; a `macro_rules!` macro only its kind, since its body is not an interface. A trait impl's methods are recorded by name only: their signatures are the trait's, recorded where the trait is. ## 5. Handles and owners The types a consumer reaches a C type through -- `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooBox`, `FooArc`, `FooVal` and a policy type such as `FooFree` -- are not always annotated. An unannotated public struct, enum, union or trait of the crate is **associated** with C items by rule 1, else by rule 2, and a type alias by rule 3; `via` says which rule tied it: 1. `assoc_type`: a trait impl of the type sets an associated type to an anchored type, or a trait impl of an anchored type sets one to it. `impl CRefSeam for MailmapRef { type Cell = Mailmap; }` and `impl CCell for Mailmap { type Ref<'a> = MailmapRef<'a>; }` both tie `MailmapRef` to `st::git_mailmap`. 2. `owner`: the type's impls, or the trait's declaration, hold stand-ins; it is associated with their C items. A policy type whose `CDrop::c_drop` wraps `fn::git_mailmap_free` goes with that item. 3. `alias`: a type alias whose target names an anchored type, by id anywhere in the target, goes with that type's C items: `MailmapBox = CBox` with `st::git_mailmap`. A target naming none goes with the items of the types it names that rules 1 and 2 associated. An associated item is recorded under each of its C items with the record a stand-in has, and a C item's surface is its stand-ins and its associated items together. ## 6. The contract view A handle or an owner changes form over a migration: `FooRef` is a pointer wrapper while `Foo` is wrapped and `&'a Foo` once it is ported, `FooBox` an ffibox `CBox` and then a `Box`. A consumer relies only on what every form offers, as `binding-types` states: their methods, their reborrows (`as_ref`, `as_mut`) and the dereferences the native forms offer. The **contract** of a type is that, and it, not the raw record, decides a C item's status. Every C item has a `contract` view: one entry per stand-in or associated item. - **A type** (`Foo`, `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooBox`, `FooArc`, `FooVal`, a policy type, an enum) has its contract under its locator: - `generics`: how many lifetimes, types and constants it takes; - `fields` (public ones), `shape` (only when a consumer can build it, no field hidden), `variants` and `non_exhaustive`; - `methods`: every method a consumer can call on it, by name, over every route: on the form itself, through its dereferences (`&self` methods through `Deref`, `&mut self` ones too through `DerefMut`) and on what its reborrows return. The route is not recorded, and the first found names a method; - `reborrows`: what `as_ref` and `as_mut` return. One returning the form's own type adds nothing and is left out; - `traits`: the traits it implements that a consumer can use, with their arguments; - `derefs`: targets reached through a dereference that the contract does not look inside (a slice, `str`, a primitive, a standard type), whose methods are the standard library's. - **A method of a handle or owner** is keyed `method::`, without its owner, since a port moves it from `FooRef` to `impl Foo`, and holds its normalised signatures. - **Any other function** has its normalised signature; anything else its raw record. Signatures in a contract are normalised so that each form reads the same: a type equal to the target of one of the crate's public aliases is written as the alias, so `&'a Foo` reads `FooRef<'_>` once `FooRef<'a> = &'a Foo`; lifetimes are erased; `Self` is the type the method is called on; a projection such as `::Ref<'_>` is resolved through `Foo`'s impl; parameter names are dropped; and a `self` receiver of a `Copy` type is `&self`. **What is no part of a contract:** | left out | why | |---|---| | functions without a `self` receiver | reached through a type path, which a change of form changes | | the seams `as_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr`, `from_void_ptr`, `from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `from_c`, `into_c`, `as_c_ptr`, `from_raw`, `as_object` | the conversion between a wrapper and its raw form, ffimap's seam list | | a method with a raw pointer or `NonNull` in its signature | raw access | | `unsafe` methods | they exist because a form wraps C; an anchored one is its own C item's | | anchored methods | each is its own C item's stand-in, compared there | | every method of a plumbing crate's type (`--plumbing`, ffibox by default) but `as_ref` and `as_mut` | what one form offers beyond the native ones, such as `try_clone` or `policy` | | the traits of a plumbing crate (`CCell`, `CDrop`, `CRefSeam`, …) | plumbing | | `Drop`, `StructuralPartialEq`, `Freeze`, `UnsafeUnpin` | no consumer can use them | | `Pointer` | it formats the address: raw access | | `Deref`, `DerefMut`, `AsRef`, `AsMut`, `Borrow`, `BorrowMut` | recorded as dereferences and reborrows, and through the methods they reach | | blanket impls | they follow from the others | **Where a form's surface comes from.** A type of the crate, or of a crate given with `--dep`, answers from its impls in that crate's JSON: an impl applies when its self type matches the form, and its bounds are checked against the impl lists rustdoc records (which list the blanket impls that apply), so `impl Send for CBox` holds for `CBox` exactly when `Foo` and `FooFree` are `Send`. A standard pointer form answers from a fixed model: `&T` and `&mut T` dereference to `T`, `Box` too, with `as_ref`/`as_mut`, `Arc` and `Rc` shared, `Pin

` as `P`, and each implements `Clone`, `Copy`, `Send`, `Sync`, `Unpin`, `UnwindSafe`, `RefUnwindSafe`, `Default`, `Debug`, `Display`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord` and `Hash` under the standard library's conditions on `T`; `NonNull` and `PhantomData` are modelled for the bounds they appear in. **Unresolved.** A contract that needs what is not there -- a type of a crate whose JSON was not given, a standard type the model does not cover, a bound that cannot be decided, such as one on the free parameter of a generic alias -- lists it under `unresolved`, and that entry is compared on its raw record instead (section 10). `contract_missing_deps` names the crates whose JSON would have resolved more. ## 7. The unattributed surface A public item of the crate that is neither a stand-in nor associated is **unattributed**. It is recorded by the Rust module of its canonical path, under `unattributed`, with the same records, and compared the same way, so a change to it is reported though no C item owns it. ## 8. Coverage `coverage` counts how far the anchors reach. `public` counts the crate's reachable items by role: free items by kind, `inherent_item` and `trait_impl_item` for the items of a type's impls (blanket and synthesised impls aside), `trait_item`, `variant` and `field`. `anchored` counts those that carry an anchor. `c_items` and `c_items_by_kind` count the keys, `stand_ins` the records, `associated` and `unattributed` the items those sections hold. ## 9. The extract ```json { "api": 2, "source": {"crate": "libgit2", "crate_version": "0.1.0", "format_version": 61, "deps": ["ffibox"], "plumbing": ["ffibox"]}, "items": { "st::git_mailmap": { "anchor": "Wraps", "stand_ins": {"libgit2::…::Mailmap": {"anchor": "Wraps", "kind": "struct", "paths": ["libgit2::…::Mailmap"], "sig": {…}}}, "associated": {"libgit2::…::MailmapBox": {"kind": "type_alias", "via": ["alias"], "paths": […], "sig": {…}}}, "contract": {"libgit2::…::MailmapBox": {"kind": "type", "generics": {…}, "methods": {…}, "reborrows": {…}, "traits": […]}, …} } }, "contract_missing_deps": [], "unattributed": {"libgit2::…::odb": {"libgit2::…::OdbDataStrVec": {…}}}, "anchors": {"malformed": [], "unknown_kinds": {}, "without_alias": []}, "coverage": {…} } ``` An item's `anchor` is its stand-ins' verb, or `mixed` when they differ. `api` is the extract's own version, bumped when a rule or the shape changes, and two extracts of different versions are not compared. Keys are sorted and the JSON is indented by one, so one document gives one byte sequence. ## 10. The diff `ffimap api diff BEFORE AFTER` takes two extracts, or two rustdoc JSON documents it extracts first (with the same `--dep` and `--plumbing`), and classifies every C item by its contract view: | status | when | |---|---| | `kept` | every entry is identical | | `extended` | only additions | | `changed` | anything lost or rewritten | | `removed` | the key is gone | | `new` | the key first appears | In the contract view an entry gained, a method, a reborrow, a trait, a dereference target, a signature beside a method's others, a field of a type with hidden fields or a variant of a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum is an addition; an entry, a method, a reborrow, a trait or a signature lost or rewritten, a generics count changed, and a field or variant gained where a consumer could build or match every one, is a change. A type whose raw record moved while its contract did not is a **retarget**: the item records `retarget` with the raw declarations before and after, and stays kept. `raw_status` says when the raw view would have classified the item otherwise. `--raw` classifies by the raw records instead, and an unresolved contract entry is compared on its raw record; the raw rules, where an addition and a change are: | addition (`extended`) | change (`changed`) | |---|---| | a stand-in or an associated item | a stand-in or an associated item lost, or its kind changed | | a public path | a public path lost | | a trait impl, auto traits included | a trait impl lost, auto traits included (`Send` becoming `!Send` is both) | | an item or associated type in a trait impl | one lost, or an associated type retargeted | | an inherent member no anchor claims | a member lost or rewritten | | a provided trait item, or a required one made provided | a required trait item, or any trait item lost or rewritten | | a field of a struct with private fields | a field of one without, or any field lost or retyped | | a variant of a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum | a variant of an exhaustive enum, or any variant lost or rewritten | | | a `decl` or `impl` header rewritten: a signature, an alias target, a constant's value | An item whose anchor verb moved records it as `anchor: {before, after}`, and `anchor_moves` counts the moves, so a wrap-to-port step reads `Wraps->Replaces` whatever the status. A key gone and a key come with the same path, one of each, are one C item whose anchor kind was relabelled: it is compared as one and records `rekeyed` with its old key. The JSON form, the default, holds the `view` that decided, `totals`, `anchor_moves`, `rekeyed`, `retargeted`, `unresolved`, every C item's `status` with its `changes`, `raw_status`, `retarget` and `unresolved`, and `unattributed` with its own totals by module, always on raw records. Each change names the entry's locator, the `part` that moved (`method`, `trait`, `reborrow`, `decl`, `impl`, `member`, `path`, …), whether it was `added`, `removed` or `changed`, its `severity` (`extended` or `changed`), the values before and after, and `view: raw` when an unresolved entry was compared raw. `--format text` prints the items that are neither kept nor new, with one line per change, then the totals. `--items` restricts the C items to a list of keys, a batch's worklist, and lists those found in neither document under `missing`. The unattributed surface is reported whatever it holds, since no worklist names it. ## 11. What the measure cannot see - **What no anchor reaches.** An unannotated type that no rule of section 5 ties to an anchored one is attributed to its module, not to a C item. - **The route to a method.** A contract flattens methods over dereferences and reborrows, so a method callable directly on one form and only through `as_ref()` on another reads the same. - **Lifetimes in contracts.** They are erased, so a getter returning a borrow of the handle and one returning a borrow of its target read the same. - **Standard types beyond the model.** A form that is an `Option`, a `Vec` or any standard type other than the pointer forms is unresolved, and so is a bound on a generic alias's free parameter. - **Behaviour.** A signature that stays while what the function does changes reads as kept. - **Renamed generics.** Generic parameter names are kept in declarations, so renaming `T` or a lifetime reads as changed, except in locators, where lifetimes are erased. - **Another crate's re-exports.** A dependency that moves a definition behind an unchanged re-export renders differently, since this document has only the definition's path. - **Semver nuance.** A change is anything lost or rewritten, whether or not a consumer could tell: a bound loosened or a where-clause reordered reads as changed. A contract's impl bounds are checked against impl lists only, one impl at a time, with no inference beyond what rustdoc recorded. - **Trait-impl method signatures.** They are the trait's; a change to an unanchored, unattributed trait is reported under its module only. - **Hidden items.** Rustdoc leaves `#[doc(hidden)]` items and private ones out of its JSON, so neither they nor anchors on them are seen.

An associated item is recorded under each of its C items with the record a stand-in has, and a C item's surface is its stand-ins and its associated items together. ## 6. The contract view A handle or an owner changes form over a migration: `FooRef` is a pointer wrapper while `Foo` is wrapped and `&'a Foo` once it is ported, `FooBox` an ffibox `CBox` and then a `Box`. A consumer relies only on what every form offers, as `binding-types` states: their methods, their reborrows (`as_ref`, `as_mut`) and the dereferences the native forms offer. The **contract** of a type is that, and it, not the raw record, decides a C item's status. Every C item has a `contract` view: one entry per stand-in or associated item. - **A type** (`Foo`, `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooBox`, `FooArc`, `FooVal`, a policy type, an enum) has its contract under its locator: - `generics`: how many lifetimes, types and constants it takes; - `fields` (public ones), `shape` (only when a consumer can build it, no field hidden), `variants` and `non_exhaustive`; - `methods`: every method a consumer can call on it, by name, over every route: on the form itself, through its dereferences (`&self` methods through `Deref`, `&mut self` ones too through `DerefMut`) and on what its reborrows return. The route is not recorded, and the first found names a method; - `reborrows`: what `as_ref` and `as_mut` return. One returning the form's own type adds nothing and is left out; - `traits`: the traits it implements that a consumer can use, with their arguments; - `derefs`: targets reached through a dereference that the contract does not look inside (a slice, `str`, a primitive, a standard type), whose methods are the standard library's. - **A method of a handle or owner** is keyed `method::`, without its owner, since a port moves it from `FooRef` to `impl Foo`, and holds its normalised signatures. - **Any other function** has its normalised signature; anything else its raw record. Signatures in a contract are normalised so that each form reads the same: a type equal to the target of one of the crate's public aliases is written as the alias, so `&'a Foo` reads `FooRef<'_>` once `FooRef<'a> = &'a Foo`; lifetimes are erased; `Self` is the type the method is called on; a projection such as `::Ref<'_>` is resolved through `Foo`'s impl; parameter names are dropped; and a `self` receiver of a `Copy` type is `&self`. **What is no part of a contract:** | left out | why | |---|---| | functions without a `self` receiver | reached through a type path, which a change of form changes | | the seams `as_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr`, `from_void_ptr`, `from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `from_c`, `into_c`, `as_c_ptr`, `from_raw`, `as_object` | the conversion between a wrapper and its raw form, ffimap's seam list | | a method with a raw pointer or `NonNull` in its signature | raw access | | `unsafe` methods | they exist because a form wraps C; an anchored one is its own C item's | | anchored methods | each is its own C item's stand-in, compared there | | every method of a plumbing crate's type (`--plumbing`, ffibox by default) but `as_ref` and `as_mut` | what one form offers beyond the native ones, such as `try_clone` or `policy` | | the traits of a plumbing crate (`CCell`, `CDrop`, `CRefSeam`, …) | plumbing | | `Drop`, `StructuralPartialEq`, `Freeze`, `UnsafeUnpin` | no consumer can use them | | `Pointer` | it formats the address: raw access | | `Deref`, `DerefMut`, `AsRef`, `AsMut`, `Borrow`, `BorrowMut` | recorded as dereferences and reborrows, and through the methods they reach | | blanket impls | they follow from the others | **Where a form's surface comes from.** A type of the crate, or of a crate given with `--dep`, answers from its impls in that crate's JSON: an impl applies when its self type matches the form, and its bounds are checked against the impl lists rustdoc records (which list the blanket impls that apply), so `impl Send for CBox` holds for `CBox` exactly when `Foo` and `FooFree` are `Send`. A standard pointer form answers from a fixed model: `&T` and `&mut T` dereference to `T`, `Box` too, with `as_ref`/`as_mut`, `Arc` and `Rc` shared, `Pin

` as `P`, and each implements `Clone`, `Copy`, `Send`, `Sync`, `Unpin`, `UnwindSafe`, `RefUnwindSafe`, `Default`, `Debug`, `Display`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord` and `Hash` under the standard library's conditions on `T`; `NonNull` and `PhantomData` are modelled for the bounds they appear in. **Unresolved.** A contract that needs what is not there -- a type of a crate whose JSON was not given, a standard type the model does not cover, a bound that cannot be decided, such as one on the free parameter of a generic alias -- lists it under `unresolved`, and that entry is compared on its raw record instead (section 10). `contract_missing_deps` names the crates whose JSON would have resolved more. ## 7. The unattributed surface A public item of the crate that is neither a stand-in nor associated is **unattributed**. It is recorded by the Rust module of its canonical path, under `unattributed`, with the same records, and compared the same way, so a change to it is reported though no C item owns it. ## 8. Coverage `coverage` counts how far the anchors reach. `public` counts the crate's reachable items by role: free items by kind, `inherent_item` and `trait_impl_item` for the items of a type's impls (blanket and synthesised impls aside), `trait_item`, `variant` and `field`. `anchored` counts those that carry an anchor. `c_items` and `c_items_by_kind` count the keys, `stand_ins` the records, `associated` and `unattributed` the items those sections hold. ## 9. The extract ```json { "api": 2, "source": {"crate": "libgit2", "crate_version": "0.1.0", "format_version": 61, "deps": ["ffibox"], "plumbing": ["ffibox"]}, "items": { "st::git_mailmap": { "anchor": "Wraps", "stand_ins": {"libgit2::…::Mailmap": {"anchor": "Wraps", "kind": "struct", "paths": ["libgit2::…::Mailmap"], "sig": {…}}}, "associated": {"libgit2::…::MailmapBox": {"kind": "type_alias", "via": ["alias"], "paths": […], "sig": {…}}}, "contract": {"libgit2::…::MailmapBox": {"kind": "type", "generics": {…}, "methods": {…}, "reborrows": {…}, "traits": […]}, …} } }, "contract_missing_deps": [], "unattributed": {"libgit2::…::odb": {"libgit2::…::OdbDataStrVec": {…}}}, "anchors": {"malformed": [], "unknown_kinds": {}, "without_alias": []}, "coverage": {…} } ``` An item's `anchor` is its stand-ins' verb, or `mixed` when they differ. `api` is the extract's own version, bumped when a rule or the shape changes, and two extracts of different versions are not compared. Keys are sorted and the JSON is indented by one, so one document gives one byte sequence. ## 10. The diff `ffimap api diff BEFORE AFTER` takes two extracts, or two rustdoc JSON documents it extracts first (with the same `--dep` and `--plumbing`), and classifies every C item by its contract view: | status | when | |---|---| | `kept` | every entry is identical | | `extended` | only additions | | `changed` | anything lost or rewritten | | `removed` | the key is gone | | `new` | the key first appears | In the contract view an entry gained, a method, a reborrow, a trait, a dereference target, a signature beside a method's others, a field of a type with hidden fields or a variant of a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum is an addition; an entry, a method, a reborrow, a trait or a signature lost or rewritten, a generics count changed, and a field or variant gained where a consumer could build or match every one, is a change. A type whose raw record moved while its contract did not is a **retarget**: the item records `retarget` with the raw declarations before and after, and stays kept. `raw_status` says when the raw view would have classified the item otherwise. `--raw` classifies by the raw records instead, and an unresolved contract entry is compared on its raw record; the raw rules, where an addition and a change are: | addition (`extended`) | change (`changed`) | |---|---| | a stand-in or an associated item | a stand-in or an associated item lost, or its kind changed | | a public path | a public path lost | | a trait impl, auto traits included | a trait impl lost, auto traits included (`Send` becoming `!Send` is both) | | an item or associated type in a trait impl | one lost, or an associated type retargeted | | an inherent member no anchor claims | a member lost or rewritten | | a provided trait item, or a required one made provided | a required trait item, or any trait item lost or rewritten | | a field of a struct with private fields | a field of one without, or any field lost or retyped | | a variant of a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum | a variant of an exhaustive enum, or any variant lost or rewritten | | | a `decl` or `impl` header rewritten: a signature, an alias target, a constant's value | An item whose anchor verb moved records it as `anchor: {before, after}`, and `anchor_moves` counts the moves, so a wrap-to-port step reads `Wraps->Replaces` whatever the status. A key gone and a key come with the same path, one of each, are one C item whose anchor kind was relabelled: it is compared as one and records `rekeyed` with its old key. The JSON form, the default, holds the `view` that decided, `totals`, `anchor_moves`, `rekeyed`, `retargeted`, `unresolved`, every C item's `status` with its `changes`, `raw_status`, `retarget` and `unresolved`, and `unattributed` with its own totals by module, always on raw records. Each change names the entry's locator, the `part` that moved (`method`, `trait`, `reborrow`, `decl`, `impl`, `member`, `path`, …), whether it was `added`, `removed` or `changed`, its `severity` (`extended` or `changed`), the values before and after, and `view: raw` when an unresolved entry was compared raw. `--format text` prints the items that are neither kept nor new, with one line per change, then the totals. `--items` restricts the C items to a list of keys, a batch's worklist, and lists those found in neither document under `missing`. The unattributed surface is reported whatever it holds, since no worklist names it. ## 11. What the measure cannot see - **What no anchor reaches.** An unannotated type that no rule of section 5 ties to an anchored one is attributed to its module, not to a C item. - **The route to a method.** A contract flattens methods over dereferences and reborrows, so a method callable directly on one form and only through `as_ref()` on another reads the same. - **Lifetimes in contracts.** They are erased, so a getter returning a borrow of the handle and one returning a borrow of its target read the same. - **Standard types beyond the model.** A form that is an `Option`, a `Vec` or any standard type other than the pointer forms is unresolved, and so is a bound on a generic alias's free parameter. - **Behaviour.** A signature that stays while what the function does changes reads as kept. - **Renamed generics.** Generic parameter names are kept in declarations, so renaming `T` or a lifetime reads as changed, except in locators, where lifetimes are erased. - **Another crate's re-exports.** A dependency that moves a definition behind an unchanged re-export renders differently, since this document has only the definition's path. - **Semver nuance.** A change is anything lost or rewritten, whether or not a consumer could tell: a bound loosened or a where-clause reordered reads as changed. A contract's impl bounds are checked against impl lists only, one impl at a time, with no inference beyond what rustdoc recorded. - **Trait-impl method signatures.** They are the trait's; a change to an unanchored, unattributed trait is reported under its module only. - **Hidden items.** Rustdoc leaves `#[doc(hidden)]` items and private ones out of its JSON, so neither they nor anchors on them are seen.

# wavefront

Wavefront answers deterministic queries about a C codebase, its entities, their uses and
dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.

It is the first resort for any question about the C codebase: an entity's definition,
fields or signature, its users, callers and casts, what it depends on, and the pointer
findings and lifecycle roles submitted on it are queried rather than searched for in the
source, so that each answer covers every site the traced build compiles, and every query
of one fact gets one answer. The source is read where wavefront records nothing, to read a
body, and to judge what wavefront records.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits

254 /crustify-rs/wavefront/README.md
# Wavefront

Wavefront analyzes a C codebase and schedules its units in dependency order
for translation to Rust. It extracts entities and dependencies with CodeQL,
builds a cycle-free dependency graph of the codebase's types and symbols, and
packs that graph into ordered waves of batches. Each batch can be translated
once the waves before it are complete.

Wavefront keeps its analysis simple: it infers facts from the codebase without
data-flow or points-to analysis. It is built for neuro-symbolic workflows, in
which human or LLM reasoning complements its static facts. You can state the
polymorphic and type-erased edges it cannot infer; Wavefront loads them into
the dependency graph, and its schedules order units by them. You can also
record pointer-level ownership and lifecycle properties for each type and
symbol, which Wavefront returns with their records.

## Requirements

- Python 3.13 or newer
- The [CodeQL CLI](https://github.com/github/codeql-cli-binaries), on `PATH`

## Installation

```sh
git clone https://github.com/crustify-rs/wavefront.git
cd wavefront
python -m pip install -e .
codeql pack install src/
```

## Usage

```text
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH COMMAND ...
```

`REPO_ROOT` is the root of the C repository. `--config` names its
`wavefront-config.json`; a relative path is resolved from `REPO_ROOT`.

### Configuration

```json
{
  "state_dir": ".wavefront",
  "closure": {
    "impl_files": {"included": ["src/"], "excluded": ["src/tests/"]},
    "api_headers": {"included": ["include/widget.h"]}
  },

# Wavefront

Wavefront analyzes a C codebase and schedules its units in dependency order
for translation to Rust. It extracts entities and dependencies with CodeQL,
builds a cycle-free dependency graph of the codebase's types and symbols, and
packs that graph into ordered waves of batches. Each batch can be translated
once the waves before it are complete.

Wavefront keeps its analysis simple: it infers facts from the codebase without
data-flow or points-to analysis. It is built for neuro-symbolic workflows, in
which human or LLM reasoning complements its static facts. You can state the
polymorphic and type-erased edges it cannot infer; Wavefront loads them into

symbol, which Wavefront returns with their records.

everything else, for the consumer to split.

```sh
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json schedule \

## Tests

```sh
PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

The default suite runs no CodeQL. A fixture's tests that compose, query or
schedule it read its committed tables, `tests/fixtures/<name>/codeql/`. The
tests that build each fixture's database and run the queries, checking the
queries' golden tables and that the committed tables are current, are
opt-in, and pass before a change to a query or a fixture's C lands:

```sh
WAVEFRONT_CODEQL_TESTS=1 PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

After such a change, re-extract the committed tables and review their diff:

```sh
PYTHONPATH=src python tests/regenerate_tables.py [FIXTURE ...]
```

# Findings schema

Field meaning for findings: the judgements a user records about an entity,
which wavefront cannot derive from the source. Every type and symbol record
that `query` prints has two parts:

```json
{"composed": {}, "findings": {}, "_analysis": {}}
```

`composed` is what wavefront derives from the CodeQL tables
([`types.md`](types.md), [`syms.md`](syms.md)). `findings` lists every slot a
user may fill for the entity, with `null` where nothing is recorded, in
exactly the shape `--update` accepts:

```sh
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH query functions --name widget_new --update findings.json
```

A user can therefore copy a record's `findings`, fill it in, and submit it.
[`examples/findings.json`](../../examples/findings.json) holds a filled
example of each kind. `--update` validates the whole document against the
composed record and applies nothing if any rule fails; the error lists every
failure. Accepted findings are kept in the ownership store
([`ownership-store.md`](ownership-store.md)).

## Types

```json
{
  "_comment_user": "...",
  "fields": {
    "<field name>": {"ptr": {}, "refcount": false, "locked_by": null}
  }
}
```

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `_comment_user` | Free-text note on the type: the reasoning behind its findings. |
| `fields` | One entry per declared field, keyed by the field's name. |
| `fields.<name>.ptr` | The field's pointer properties ([`pointer-properties.md`](../pointer-properties.md)); pointer fields only. |
| `fields.<name>.refcount` | `true` on the one field that stores the type's reference count: the value an up-ref increments and a down-ref decrements ([`type-lifecycle.md`](../type-lifecycle.md)). |
| `fields.<name>.locked_by` | The lock that guards the field, pointer or not: `null`, or a [lock binding](#lock-binding). |

A type has no lifecycle slot. Its lifecycle routines record their roles on
their own symbol records.

## Symbols

The slots depend on the symbol's kind.

**Functions and callbacks:**

```json
{
  "ptr_args": {"<arg name>": {"ptr": {}}},
  "ptr_ret": {"ptr": {}},
  "lifetime": null
}
```

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `ptr_args` | One entry per pointer parameter, keyed by the parameter's name (never its position). |
| `ptr_args.<name>.ptr` | The parameter's pointer properties. |
| `ptr_ret.ptr` | The returned pointer's properties; present only when the symbol returns a pointer. |
| `lifetime` | The symbol's [lifecycle role](#lifetime), or `null`. |

**Callbacks** take `forks` as well: see [Forks](#forks).

**Globals:**

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `ptr` | The global's pointer properties, when it stores a pointer; `null` otherwise. |
| `locked_by` | The lock that guards the global: `null`, or a [lock binding](#lock-binding). |

**Macros** take no findings.

A symbol has no note slot: the reasoning behind a pointer's properties goes
in that pointer's `ptr.note`.

### lifetime

The lifecycle role the symbol plays, and the object it acts on.

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `for` | The parameter the role acts on, by name (`s`, not `arg:s` or a position); or `"return"` for an `alloc` constructor that returns its object. |
| `is_dropper` | The symbol frees the object's own storage: a full destructor. |
| `is_disposer` | The symbol frees what the object's fields own, and keeps the object's storage: a cleanup or reset. |
| `is_cloner` | `null`, or `{deep, upref}`: the symbol copies the object. `deep` is a new, independent allocation; `upref` a reference-count increment that returns the same object. Both may be set when the copy depends on the path taken. |
| `is_constructor` | `null`, or `{alloc, init}`: the symbol produces an object. `alloc` hands the caller a new object it owns, returned or stored through a `T **` out-parameter; `init` initializes caller-provided storage in place. Exactly one is set. |

`--update` rejects a `lifetime` block unless:

- it sets at least one role; `null` states that the symbol has none;
- `for` names one of the symbol's pointer parameters, or is `"return"` on an
  `alloc` constructor that returns a pointer;
- an `alloc` through a parameter names a `T **` (depth 2 or more), and an
  `init` a `T *` (depth 1);
- `is_dropper` and `is_disposer` are not both set, and a constructor sets no
  other role;
- the mode flags of `is_cloner` and `is_constructor` are booleans, and
  `alloc` and `init` are not both set;
- the subject's pointer properties agree: a dropper's argument is owned, a
  cloner's is borrowed, an `alloc` constructor's return is owned, and a
  constructor's argument is not immutable.

The last rule reads the subject's `ptr` as it stands after the update, and is
skipped while that `ptr` is `null`. [`type-lifecycle.md`](../type-lifecycle.md)
describes the roles and how to find the routines that play them.

### Forks

A callback whose invokers realize different contracts is split into forks:
one record per contract, each with its own pointer properties and role. On
the callback's primary record, `forks` lists them:

```json
{
  "forks": [
    {"ptr_args": {}, "ptr_ret": {}, "lifetime": null, "callsites": ["<invoker>"]}
  ]
}
```

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `forks[].ptr_args`, `ptr_ret`, `lifetime` | The fork's own findings, as on the primary. |
| `forks[].callsites` | The invokers that realize this fork's contract; the primary keeps the rest. Each invoker belongs to at most one fork. |

Each fork's own record shows its findings with its `callsites`. Forks are
submitted through the primary's `forks`, which replaces every earlier fork.

## Lock binding

`locked_by` names the lock that guards a field or a global:

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `lock` | The field or global that stores the lock object. |
| `lock_op` | The routines that acquire it. Which ones appear shows how readers and writers lock. |
| `unlock_op` | The routines that release it. |

## Merging

`--update` merges a submission into what is already recorded:

- a type's fields merge one by one, and each named key replaces its value;
  `_comment_user` is replaced when present;
- a symbol's parameters merge one by one, and a `ptr` block replaces the
  previous one entirely, so it must be complete;
- a `null` slot clears what was recorded: a field's or a parameter's `ptr`,
  the return's `ptr`, a global's `ptr`, `lifetime`, and `locked_by`;
- a slot the submission omits is left as it is;
- `forks` replaces every earlier fork of the callback.

Submitting a record's own `findings` unchanged therefore leaves every
recorded value as it is, and `null` is how a wrong finding is withdrawn.

queries' golden tables and that the committed tables are current, are
opt-in, and pass before a change to a query or a fixture's C lands:

# Findings schema

Field meaning for findings: the judgements a user records about an entity,
which wavefront cannot derive from the source. Every type and symbol record
that `query` prints has two parts:

```json
{"composed": {}, "findings": {}, "_analysis": {}}
```

`composed` is what wavefront derives from the CodeQL tables
([`types.md`](types.md), [`syms.md`](syms.md)). `findings` lists every slot a
user may fill for the entity, with `null` where nothing is recorded, in
exactly the shape `--update` accepts:

```sh
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH query functions --name widget_new --update findings.json
```

A user can therefore copy a record's `findings`, fill it in, and submit it.
[`examples/findings.json`](../../examples/findings.json) holds a filled
example of each kind. `--update` validates the whole document against the
composed record and applies nothing if any rule fails; the error lists every
failure. Accepted findings are kept in the ownership store
([`ownership-store.md`](ownership-store.md)).

## Types

```json
{
  "_comment_user": "...",
  "fields": {
    "<field name>": {"ptr": {}, "refcount": false, "locked_by": null}
  }
}
```

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `_comment_user` | Free-text note on the type: the reasoning behind its findings. |
| `fields` | One entry per declared field, keyed by the field's name. |
| `fields.<name>.ptr` | The field's pointer properties ([`pointer-properties.md`](../pointer-properties.md)); pointer fields only. |
| `fields.<name>.refcount` | `true` on the one field that stores the type's reference count: the value an up-ref increments and a down-ref decrements ([`type-lifecycle.md`](../type-lifecycle.md)). |
| `fields.<name>.locked_by` | The lock that guards the field, pointer or not: `null`, or a [lock binding](#lock-binding). |

A type has no lifecycle slot. Its lifecycle routines record their roles on
their own symbol records.

## Symbols

The slots depend on the symbol's kind.

**Functions and callbacks:**

```json
{
  "ptr_args": {"<arg name>": {"ptr": {}}},
  "ptr_ret": {"ptr": {}},
  "lifetime": null
}
```

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `ptr_args` | One entry per pointer parameter, keyed by the parameter's name (never its position). |
| `ptr_args.<name>.ptr` | The parameter's pointer properties. |
| `ptr_ret.ptr` | The returned pointer's properties; present only when the symbol returns a pointer. |
| `lifetime` | The symbol's [lifecycle role](#lifetime), or `null`. |

**Callbacks** take `forks` as well: see [Forks](#forks).

**Globals:**

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `ptr` | The global's pointer properties, when it stores a pointer; `null` otherwise. |
| `locked_by` | The lock that guards the global: `null`, or a [lock binding](#lock-binding). |

**Macros** take no findings.

A symbol has no note slot: the reasoning behind a pointer's properties goes
in that pointer's `ptr.note`.

### lifetime

The lifecycle role the symbol plays, and the object it acts on.

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `for` | The parameter the role acts on, by name (`s`, not `arg:s` or a position); or `"return"` for an `alloc` constructor that returns its object. |
| `is_dropper` | The symbol frees the object's own storage: a full destructor. |
| `is_disposer` | The symbol frees what the object's fields own, and keeps the object's storage: a cleanup or reset. |
| `is_cloner` | `null`, or `{deep, upref}`: the symbol copies the object. `deep` is a new, independent allocation; `upref` a reference-count increment that returns the same object. Both may be set when the copy depends on the path taken. |
| `is_constructor` | `null`, or `{alloc, init}`: the symbol produces an object. `alloc` hands the caller a new object it owns, returned or stored through a `T **` out-parameter; `init` initializes caller-provided storage in place. Exactly one is set. |

`--update` rejects a `lifetime` block unless:

- it sets at least one role; `null` states that the symbol has none;
- `for` names one of the symbol's pointer parameters, or is `"return"` on an
  `alloc` constructor that returns a pointer;
- an `alloc` through a parameter names a `T **` (depth 2 or more), and an
  `init` a `T *` (depth 1);
- `is_dropper` and `is_disposer` are not both set, and a constructor sets no
  other role;
- the mode flags of `is_cloner` and `is_constructor` are booleans, and
  `alloc` and `init` are not both set;
- the subject's pointer properties agree: a dropper's argument is owned, a
  cloner's is borrowed, an `alloc` constructor's return is owned, and a
  constructor's argument is not immutable.

The last rule reads the subject's `ptr` as it stands after the update, and is
skipped while that `ptr` is `null`. [`type-lifecycle.md`](../type-lifecycle.md)
describes the roles and how to find the routines that play them.

### Forks

A callback whose invokers realize different contracts is split into forks:
one record per contract, each with its own pointer properties and role. On
the callback's primary record, `forks` lists them:

```json
{
  "forks": [
    {"ptr_args": {}, "ptr_ret": {}, "lifetime": null, "callsites": ["<invoker>"]}
  ]
}
```

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `forks[].ptr_args`, `ptr_ret`, `lifetime` | The fork's own findings, as on the primary. |
| `forks[].callsites` | The invokers that realize this fork's contract; the primary keeps the rest. Each invoker belongs to at most one fork. |

Each fork's own record shows its findings with its `callsites`. Forks are
submitted through the primary's `forks`, which replaces every earlier fork.

## Lock binding

`locked_by` names the lock that guards a field or a global:

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `lock` | The field or global that stores the lock object. |
| `lock_op` | The routines that acquire it. Which ones appear shows how readers and writers lock. |
| `unlock_op` | The routines that release it. |

## Merging

`--update` merges a submission into what is already recorded:

- a type's fields merge one by one, and each named key replaces its value;
  `_comment_user` is replaced when present;
- a symbol's parameters merge one by one, and a `ptr` block replaces the
  previous one entirely, so it must be complete;
- a `null` slot clears what was recorded: a field's or a parameter's `ptr`,
  the return's `ptr`, a global's `ptr`, `lifetime`, and `locked_by`;
- a slot the submission omits is left as it is;
- `forks` replaces every earlier fork of the callback.

Submitting a record's own `findings` unchanged therefore leaves every
recorded value as it is, and `null` is how a wrong finding is withdrawn.

---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |

The lessons are reconciled at each ship point, and whenever five have been added or changed
since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
is `provisional` again.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. A change is finished once its proposal names its commit. A finished
change is reviewed before the next wave of its campaign launches, so that later runs work on
the fix rather than around it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- the row its proposal drafts for the record, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes, names a recurrence
  signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. A rebase of a change to
the text of skills, agents or templates alone, no script or program among its files, is the
exception, where each file the commit changes is the same in the rebased commit and its
parent as in the reviewed commit and its parent: the review then read the same diff against
the same text. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided changes no rule and is not reviewed: a row of the index,
a status of the record, or a proposal's status, verdict and review. A row of the record is
reviewed in its proposal, with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the index's rows and the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it, without
the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else runs on it.

The protected paths are the exception. They hold what judges the work, and a run that can
loosen what judges it passes by loosening it. In Crustify's repository they are:

- `GOALS.md`;
- `skills/crustify/evolution/**` and `skills/verification/**`, the scripts beside those
  skills included;
- `skills/artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md`;
- the Lints and Unsafe code sections of `skills/rust/toolchain/SKILL.md`;
- the Testing, Reviewing and Audit sections of `skills/tools/*/SKILL.md`, and every section
  of one that describes a scan a landing passes, such as `ffimap`'s Binding › Safe boundary;
- `agents/common.md`, `agents/reviewer.md` and the Evolution section of
  `agents/assistant/assistant.md`;
- the `evolution` question of `templates/*/CRUSTIFY.template.md`;
- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, which decides the skills and hooks a run loads; and
- `providers/generic/compose.py` and, under `providers/claude/`, `compose.py`, `spawn.py`,
  `system-prompt.md`, `hooks.json` and `agents/*.md`. A generated agent that changes only as
  its sources outside this list changed is not a change to a protected path.

A change whose diff touches a protected path lands on the working branch only with the
user's approval, whatever its review says, and so does the removal of a `weakens a check`
mark from the record. One case lands without that approval: the repair of a defect in
protected code, a script or a provider's program, that blocks the campaign, once its review
approves it and finds three things. The repair weakens no check. Every existing test of the
code it touches is unchanged. The repair adds a regression test of its own. Such a repair is
put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
user. A
change to `GOALS.md` is proposed and never made, unless the user asks for it, since
`GOALS.md` is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: open proposals are landed
as the autonomy allows, the working branches are offered to the user for `devel`, and the
revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled. The
lessons are reconciled when [Lessons](#5-lessons) times it, and the record's rows are read
when [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) times it.

## 11. The record

The record of what landed, `EVOLUTION.md`, and how evolution itself evolves from it are
[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

| `propose` | nothing but the index's rows and the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it, without
the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else runs on it.

The protected paths are the exception. They hold what judges the work, and a run that can
loosen what judges it passes by loosening it. In Crustify's repository they are:

- `GOALS.md`;
- `skills/crustify/evolution/**` and `skills/verification/**`, the scripts beside those
  skills included;
- `skills/artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md`;
- the Lints and Unsafe code sections of `skills/rust/toolchain/SKILL.md`;
- the Testing, Reviewing and Audit sections of `skills/tools/*/SKILL.md`, and every section
  of one that describes a scan a landing passes, such as `ffimap`'s Binding › Safe boundary;
- `agents/common.md`, `agents/reviewer.md` and the Evolution section of
  `agents/assistant/assistant.md`;
- the `evolution` question of `templates/*/CRUSTIFY.template.md`;
- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, which decides the skills and hooks a run loads; and
- `providers/generic/compose.py` and, under `providers/claude/`, `compose.py`, `spawn.py`,
  `system-prompt.md`, `hooks.json` and `agents/*.md`. A generated agent that changes only as
  its sources outside this list changed is not a change to a protected path.

A change whose diff touches a protected path lands on the working branch only with the
user's approval, whatever its review says, and so does the removal of a `weakens a check`
mark from the record. One case lands without that approval: the repair of a defect in
protected code, a script or a provider's program, that blocks the campaign, once its review
approves it and finds three things. The repair weakens no check. Every existing test of the
code it touches is unchanged. The repair adds a regression test of its own. Such a repair is
put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
user. A
change to `GOALS.md` is proposed and never made, unless the user asks for it, since
`GOALS.md` is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: open proposals are landed
as the autonomy allows, the working branches are offered to the user for `devel`, and the
revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled. The
lessons are reconciled when [Lessons](#5-lessons) times it, and the record's rows are read
when [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) times it.

## 11. The record

The record of what landed, `EVOLUTION.md`, and how evolution itself evolves from it are
[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

---
name: evolution-record
description: "The record of the changes that landed in Crustify and its tools, `EVOLUTION.md`: its rows, their recurrence signals and statuses, when the watched rows are read, and how evolution itself evolves from the record. Read before drafting a change's row, writing or reading the record, or proposing a change to the evolution protocol."
---

# Evolution record

The record of what [`evolution`](../SKILL.md) landed, and what evolution learns from it.

## 1. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. A row gives the campaign and proposal the change came
from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence signal
and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change no
proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came from.
A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.

A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
  it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

A row's signal is looked for at two times, in every campaign:

- when a proposal is indexed, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Proposals section describes:
  a signal that matches a row's recurrence signal marks that row `recurred`; and
- periodically, when the rows still `watched` are read against the findings, failed runs,
  proposals and corrections since the last reading. The campaign sets the period from its
  state, shorter after a change to a check lands or while findings cluster, longer while
  its modules are small: by default, after every fifth module it integrates. The rows are
  always read at each ship point and at an audit's end.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign and reaches `devel`
with it. Rows are appended in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge
of two campaigns' working branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the readings still run and their statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, they do not run.

## 2. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Signals section lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Autonomy section describes.

---
name: authoring
description: "How Crustify itself is organized: skills, roles, tool skills and the plugin, where each kind of text goes, and the language every text is written in. Read before changing Crustify, filing a proposal or a lesson, or writing a task message for an agent."
---
# Authoring
How Crustify is organized: its skills, its agents and the providers that serve them to an
agent host, and where each kind of text lives. The aim is that every rule is written once,
in the one place its kind belongs, so that changing it changes every agent that follows it,
and no two copies drift apart.
## 1. Layers
Crustify is text in three layers, with one more per run:
| layer | where | voice | holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| skills | `skills/<group>/<name>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what Crustify's artifacts are and how its work is done: workflows, how-tos, conventions, schemas |
| tool skills | `skills/tools/<tool>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what each tool is, and how it serves each stage |
| agents | `agents/<agent>.md`, with `agents/common.md`, and the assistant's under `agents/assistant/` | instructive, second person | an agent's identity, inputs, what it owns, its steps and what its role changes in the skill index |
| task messages | `task.md` beside a run's `task.json` | instructive | what one run is given: its inputs, and what it needs beyond its role |
Each artifact's schema, the meaning of its fields, is a skill under `skills/artifacts/`,
and an example of each is given under `templates/`, which the schema cites. The settings,
dashboard and `.gitignore` templates there are what a campaign copies to start. Examples
hold illustrations, not rules.
The layers are plain Markdown, so that any agent reads them as files. A provider, under
`providers/<host>/`, serves them to one agent host in its own format, as
[Providers](#4-providers) describes; the layers name no host.
### 1.1 Skills
A skill describes. It states what an artifact holds, how a decision is made, what a
procedure produces and when each of its steps happens, never what an agent should do, and
never who does a step: which agent owns which step is the agents'. It does not name the
tools that serve it either: a skill reads the same whether or not a tool is installed, so
a statement such as "each unit's lifecycle role is established while planning" belongs in
a skill, and the wavefront command that records it belongs in wavefront's tool skill.
Skills are grouped by the part of the work they describe: `workflows/`, `planning/`,
`rust/`, `verification/`, `operations/`, `artifacts/`, `tools/` and `crustify/`. A skill's
name is unique across the groups, since agents invoke it by name. Two kinds of skill
describe how work is done. A how-to, such as `binding` or `porting`, describes how one item
is handled. A workflow, under `workflows/`, describes how one kind of campaign proceeds
from its settings to its results: `setup`, which every campaign shares, and one per kind of
campaign (`binding-workflow`, `porting-workflow`, `audit-workflow`). A workflow names the
how-tos and the layout rather than restating them.
A skill opens with frontmatter that gives its `name` and its `description`. The
description is all an agent sees of the skill before it reads it, so it says what the skill
covers and before which step it is read. A skill stays under about 4,500 tokens, so that a
host that brings an invoked skill back after compacting an agent's context brings it back
whole; one that outgrows that is split at a section that another step needs on its own.
The parts sit in sub-directories of the skill's own, `skills/<group>/<skill>/<part>/SKILL.md`,
each named `<skill>-<part>`, and the skill's own `SKILL.md` keeps what they share: `binding`
and `porting` keep their boundaries, and their `-types` and `-symbols` parts their routes.
A skill's directory may also hold a script the skill describes, with its tests beside it,
standard library only, so that it runs wherever the skill is read: `usage` holds
`crustify-usage`.
A skill or an agent says what a step does and which program does it, never the program's
command lines, flags or options, which change with the program: the program's own `--help`
and documentation give them, and the text sends its reader there. A command appears only
where its exact form is what must hold, and a procedure of several commands that must run
exactly so is a script beside its skill, documented by its own `--help`.
Every skill's sections are numbered. A reference to a section names it, with or without its
number ("testing-builds' Coverage section", "layout § Lifecycle › Waves"), so that a renumbering
never silently points a reference at another section. A skill links another by its
relative path, with the other's name as the link's text.
### 1.2 Agents
An agent instructs. Its file holds what is specific to it: its place among the agents, its
inputs, its workflow steps, and the guidelines that apply to one step or stage. Where a step
follows a skill, the agent names the skill's section rather than restating it ("as the
`scheduling` skill's Order section describes"); where a step adds to it, the agent states
only the addition.
An agent states what it owns by naming the skill sections it carries out ("you create and
purge every level of the `layout` skill's Lifecycle section"), and adds only what the
skills leave to it: the commands it runs, the judgements it makes, the cases it must not
handle itself.
Every agent's prompt opens with `agents/common.md`: that every commit takes the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives, that a task
message's instructions take precedence over the rest of the prompt, except where a skill or a
role says a task message adds to a check and never relaxes it, and how skills and
tool skills are read. Every agent sees every skill, with its description:

# Where a symbol alias's anchor goes

Status: `landed`, Crustify `107cc09` (`devel`)

## Signal

A rule an agent had to work out by hand that a skill should state. `binding-symbols`'
Macros section binds a symbol alias "through the safe wrapper of the symbol it names", and
the conventions' What is annotated section puts a macro's anchor on "the generic, `const`,
function or `macro_rules!` that stands in for it". Neither says where the anchor of an
alias goes when the symbol it names has no wrapper of its own: a lifecycle primitive of a
foundational module, which the Lifecycle strategies section binds as strategy methods and
never as an ordinary safe function.

## Evidence

`foundational/libgit2/src/util/alloc.c/wave-177/batch-0/run-1` bound xdiff's
`xdl_malloc`, `xdl_calloc`, `xdl_realloc` and `xdl_free` (`deps/xdiff/git-xdiff.h`), each
`#define`d as one of `git__malloc`, `git__calloc`, `git__realloc` and `git__free`. The
first, second and fourth stand in Rust as `CAlloc::c_alloc`, `CLenAlloc::c_alloc_len`,
`CLenClone::c_clone_len`, `CAllocZeroed::c_alloc_zeroed`, `ArrayFree::new_zeroed` and the
three `c_drop`s of `src/libgit2/src/util/alloc.rs`. The run anchored each macro beside its
primitive's anchor on every one of those stand-ins (`mac::xdl_malloc` beside
`fn::git__malloc`, and so on), and `xdl_realloc` beside `fn::git__realloc` on
`ArrayFree::resize_bytes`; `ffimap api` keys all four as `new` items with those stand-ins.

## Destination and change

The spec, `binding-symbols`' Macros section, which the binder evolves: a symbol alias's
stand-ins are those of the symbol it names, each carrying the alias's anchor beside the
symbol's own, the strategy methods where the symbol is a lifecycle primitive.

## Validation

By the evidence that motivated it: the run above bound the four macros so, and its
`ffimap api` measure attributes each to its stand-ins.
